flag.text: Nationalists led by Messali Hadj flew this flag in the 1930s, and the National Liberation Front carried it through the war of independence. It became the national flag in 1962 and a law of April 1963 fixed its design but gave no meaning. Green is traditionally linked to Islam and white to peace and purity; red is often said to recall those who died for freedom, and the crescent and star are long-used symbols of Islam.

reasons.feature: Green left half and white right half
reasons.why: Green is traditionally read as Islam and white as peace or purity; some writers also link white to Emir Abdelkader's white flag of the 1840s. No law assigns meanings.

reasons.feature: Red crescent and five-pointed star in the center
reasons.why: Crescent and star are long-standing symbols of Islam; red is popularly said to recall the blood of those who died for independence, and the star's five points are sometimes linked to the five pillars of Islam.

Flown by Messali Hadj's nationalist movement in the 1930s (first copy often credited to Emilie Busquant in 1934, though some historians cite 1919-1920 demonstrations), adopted by the FLN and by the provisional government in 1958; the designer remains uncertain.
Became the national flag at independence on 3 July 1962; Law No. 63-145 of 25 April 1963 standardized the design without stating a meaning for the colors.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population is the WPP 2024 mid-2024 medium-variant figure as reproduced by Worldometer (the UN API was not reachable). Color meanings are traditional only; no official text giving a meaning was found (the Algerian embassy page surfaced by search was unreachable). Reviewer confirmed the flag image shows only the green and white halves plus the red crescent and star, all covered in the text.

funFact.note: Wikipedia: hometown of Septimius Severus; ruins 130 km east of Tripoli; 'among the best-preserved Roman sites in the Mediterranean'.

flag.text: Omar Faiek Shennib designed this flag for the kingdom of Libya, independent in 1951. The black band with a white crescent and star comes from the banner of the Senussi rulers of eastern Libya. Shennib said red recalls blood shed for freedom, black the dark years of Italian rule, green farming and future wealth, the crescent the Islamic calendar and the star hope. Replaced after 1969, it was brought back in the 2011 uprising.

reasons.feature: Wide black middle band with white crescent and star
reasons.why: Taken from the black banner with crescent and star of the Senussi dynasty of Cyrenaica (eastern Libya), whose leader became King Idris.

reasons.feature: Red top band, black middle band, green bottom band
reasons.why: Designer Omar Faiek Shennib, as reported by his daughters and an official Kingdom of Libya booklet, said red stands for blood sacrificed for freedom, black for the dark days under Italian occupation, and green for agriculture and future prosperity.

reasons.feature: The three colors and Libya's three regions
reasons.why: The colors are also said to echo the three historic regions: red for Fezzan, black for Cyrenaica and green for Tripolitania.
Per the Kingdom of Libya booklet, the crescent marks the start of the lunar month of the Islamic calendar and the star stands for hope and faith in God.

Adopted 24 December 1951 at independence; replaced after the 1969 coup and from 1977 by a plain green flag; readopted by the National Transitional Council on 27 February 2011 and written into the 2011 Constitutional Declaration, which specifies the red, black and green stripes.

entries.remainingDoubts: Drive side rests on one source after the Wikipedia table was truncated. Population is WPP 2024 mid-2024 via Worldometer's reproduction. The designer's color meanings come from family interviews and a kingdom booklet cited on Wikipedia, not from a flag law. Reviewer confirmed the flag image (red, double-width black, green bands; white crescent and star) is fully covered by the text.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia area list: 1,878,000 (land 1,868,000 plus inland water 10,010), re-verified by the reviewer on the list page. The Sudan country infobox gives 1,886,068; the area list value is used as the rules require.

languages.note: Arabic and English per infobox; established as official working languages by the 2005 Interim National Constitution (Languages of Sudan article, re-checked by the reviewer). funFact.value: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: the kings and queens of Kush built around 255 steep-sided pyramids at Meroë, Nuri and other sites along the Nile.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: approximately 255 Nubian pyramids, more than double the number built in ancient Egypt, at El-Kurru, Nuri, Jebel Barkal and Meroë.

driveSide.note: RHT in both sources; Wikipedia notes Sudan switched to right-hand traffic in 1973. Agrees with seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Sudan chose this flag in 1970 through a design competition won by artist Abdel Rahman Ahmed Al-Jali. Red, white, black and green are the Pan-Arab colors, laid out like the Arab Liberation flag that began in Egypt; the green triangle makes it Sudan's own. The colors are often read as red for struggle and sacrifice, white for peace, black for the country's name, which means land of the black people in Arabic, and green for Islam and farmland.

reasons.feature: Red, white and black horizontal bands
reasons.why: These are the Pan-Arab colors in the Arab Liberation layout that began with Egypt's 1952 revolution; such flags keep red-white-black bands and use green to tell them apart.

reasons.feature: Green triangle at the left edge
reasons.why: Green is the fourth Pan-Arab color, placed as a triangle to distinguish Sudan's flag from the other Arab Liberation flags; popularly read as Islam, agriculture and prosperity.

reasons.feature: Meanings of red, white and black
reasons.why: Popular readings, cited on Wikipedia from World Flags 101 rather than from a law: red for the independence struggle and sacrifice, white for peace, light and optimism (and the White Flag League), black for the country's name (Arabic for land of the black people).
Adopted 20 May 1970 after a 1969 change of government, via a public design competition won by Abdel Rahman Ahmed Al-Jali; it replaced the blue-yellow-green independence flag of 1956.

entries.remainingDoubts: Area differs between Wikipedia's area list (1,878,000, confirmed by the reviewer) and the country infobox (1,886,068); the list value was used per the rules. Color meanings are popular readings, not from a flag law. Official-language basis confirmed only for the 2005 Interim Constitution; the Languages of Sudan article does not cover the 2019 Constitutional Declaration. Population is WPP 2024 mid-2024 via Worldometer's reproduction. Reviewer confirmed the flag image (red, white, black bands with a green triangle at the left) is fully covered by the text.

entries.name: Tunisia

officialName.note: Wikipedia infobox and lead give the English official name as Republic of Tunisia; re-confirmed on the Tunisia article in this check.

capital.note: Single capital per the seed's ownerRules and the Wikipedia infobox (Tunis, 36 49 N 10 11 E), re-confirmed in this check.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, medium variant, 1 July 2024 estimate 12,277,109 (Worldometers yearly table, which states it is based on World Population Prospects: The 2024 Revision), rounded to 3 significant figures. The Wikipedia UN table only shows 2022 (12,119,334) and 2023 (12,200,431) columns, consistent with this figure. Tunisia's own 2024 census counted a lower 11,972,169; the UN figure is used as the rules require.

areaSqKm.note: Total area including land (155,360 km2) and inland water (8,250 km2) per Wikipedia's list; the Tunisia infobox gives the same 163,610 km2 total with 5.04% water.

languages.note: Infobox lists Modern Standard Arabic as the sole official language; written as Arabic per ownerRules. Tunisian Arabic (vernacular) and French are widely spoken but not official, so excluded.

currency.note: Infobox gives Tunisian dinar (TND), re-confirmed in this check. The local abbreviation DT is also common; the ISO code is used here as the opened source states it.

landmarks.note: The Tunisia article names the archaeological site of Carthage, the Great Mosque of Kairouan and the Amphitheatre of El Jem. The El Jem article confirms it is a Roman amphitheatre built around 238 AD in El Djem, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979, with an estimated capacity of 35,000.

funFact.value: Tunisia holds Cape Angela, the northernmost point of mainland Africa, and the ruins of ancient Carthage, Rome's great rival, lie beside its capital Tunis.
funFact.note: 154 characters. The Tunisia article states the country holds Africa's northernmost point, Cape Angela, and the archaeological sites of Carthage dating to the 9th century BC; Carthage's rivalry with Rome (the Punic Wars) is standard history. Carthage is a suburb within greater Tunis.

driveSide.note: Right-hand traffic per the traffic-side table and the Tunisia infobox (driving side: right), matching the seed's leftHand=false. No source disagreed.

flag.text: Hussein II Bey created the flag around 1831 so Tunisian ships stood out from those of the Ottoman Empire, which then ruled Tunisia. Its red background, crescent and star follow the Ottoman flag. Tunisia's embassy in France says red recalls the blood of its martyrs, the white disc means peace, the crescent Muslim unity and the five star points the five pillars of Islam. The constitution and a 1999 law set its design.

reasons.feature: Overall design: red background with a white disc holding a red crescent and five-pointed star
reasons.why: Designed by Bey Hussein II after the Battle of Navarino (20 October 1827), where the Tunisian fleet was lost, so Tunisian ships could be distinguished from Ottoman ones; the Tunisian government gives the adoption year as 1831, while some sources say 1835. The red color with crescent and star follows the flag of the Ottoman Empire, of which Tunisia was then a province. The design survived the French protectorate unchanged. Confirmed against the flag image: red background, white disc, red crescent, red five-pointed star, nothing else.

According to the Tunisian embassy in France (as quoted in the Wikipedia article), red represents the blood of Tunisian martyrs killed during the Crusades before the advent of the Ottomans in 1574. No law assigns this meaning; the 1999 law covers only the design, colors and proportions.
The embassy explanation gives white as peace and the disc as the radiance of the nation as the sun.

The embassy explanation gives the crescent as the unity of all Muslims. The article also notes the crescent appeared on Carthaginian standards before Islam (Whitney Smith traces it to ancient Carthage), so it may be an older regional symbol as well as an Islamic one.
The embassy explanation gives the five points as the Five Pillars of Islam.

reasons.feature: Crescent and star as a shared motif
reasons.why: Traditionally seen across many Muslim-majority countries' flags as symbols of Islam, inherited from Ottoman usage; the article notes they may be cultural rather than exclusively religious symbols. The text names the Ottoman origin.

Article 4 of the 1 June 1959 Constitution: the flag of the Republic of Tunisia is red and has, under conditions defined by law, in the middle a white disk containing a five-pointed star surrounded by a red crescent. Organic Law No. 99-56 of 30 June 1999 fixed exact proportions, color values and geometry for the first time. A web search snippet gave Article 4 of the 2022 constitution with the same description (red, white circle, five-pointed star surrounded by a red crescent, as provided for by law), but that page was not opened.

entries.remainingDoubts: Adoption year is given as 1831 by the Tunisian government and most sources but 1835 by some; the text says around 1831. The color meanings come from the Tunisian embassy in France as quoted by Wikipedia; the embassy page itself was not opened, and no Tunisian law gives the colors a meaning. The 2022 constitution's flag article (Article 4, same description) was seen only in a web search snippet, not on an opened page. The 2024 population figure comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 (12,277,109), not from the UN data portal directly; the Wikipedia UN table shows only 2022 and 2023 columns. Currency symbol: TND (ISO) used; DT is the common local abbreviation.

funFact.value: The Kingdom of Dahomey, which ruled this land before the French, was famous for its elite units of female soldiers, known in Europe as the Dahomey Amazons.
funFact.note: Wikipedia Benin article: Dahomey's elite female soldier corps, the Dahomean Amazons. 155 characters.

driveSide.note: RHT per Wikipedia table; matches seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Adopted in 1959, just before independence from France, the flag uses green, yellow and red, Pan-African colors taken from Ethiopia's flag. The national anthem gives the official meaning: green for the hope of renewal, red for the courage of the ancestors, yellow for the country's riches. A Marxist government flew a green flag with a red star from 1975 to 1990; the old flag returned with democracy and is written into the 1990 constitution.

reasons.feature: Green vertical band next to the pole with yellow over red bands beside it
reasons.why: Design first adopted 16 November 1959 before independence; Constitution of 1990 Article 1 fixes the layout (green band two-fifths of the length, yellow above red).
Pan-African colors derived from Ethiopia's flag and used by the African Democratic Rally across French West Africa during decolonization; shared with many African nations.

reasons.feature: Meaning of green, red and yellow
reasons.why: The national anthem L'Aube Nouvelle (adopted 1960) states: in the green you read the hope of renewal, red evokes the courage of the ancestors, yellow foretells the richest treasures. Wikipedia's flag article cites the anthem as the source of the meaning.

People's Republic of Benin used a green flag with a red star in the upper left corner after the 1972 coup (never adopted by law, so only the de facto flag); the original flag was restored 1 August 1990 with multi-party democracy.

entries.remainingDoubts: Ganvié as third landmark not verified in an opened source (well known, but choose another if strict sourcing is needed). Population figure taken from Worldometers' republication of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal itself; the Wikipedia UN list only shows 2022 and 2023 columns, which are consistent with it.

officialName.note: The state has no longer form; Wikipedia infobox and the constitution use simply Burkina Faso.

capital.note: Per ownerRules and Wikipedia infobox.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 medium variant: 23,548,781 (via Worldometers; UN API returned 401). Reviewer check: the Wikipedia UN list (WPP 2024) shows 23,025,776 for 1 July 2023, consistent with 23.55 million in mid-2024. 3 s.f. gives 23,500,000 and 4 s.f. gives 23,550,000, both ending in 5 followed by zeros, so rounded to 5 s.f. (23,549,000) to honor the no-trailing-5 rule; change to 23,550,000 if 4 s.f. is preferred.

languages.note: Constitutional Law 045-2023/ALT (adopted 30 Dec 2023, promulgated 22 Jan 2024) rewrote Article 35: the national languages officialised by law are the official languages; French and English are only working languages. Reviewer re-checked Wikipedia's Languages of Burkina Faso article: the amendment made the national languages official 'while not naming any of those languages', and no implementing law naming specific languages was found in any opened source. Mooré, Dyula and Fula are the three national languages officially recognised since 1998 and named in the government's proposal, so they are listed as the best available answer; French is deliberately omitted because it is no longer official. A web search for the law text surfaced the National Assembly PDF (an.bf) and Burkina24 coverage but these were not opened.

currency.note: West African CFA franc (XOF) per infobox.

landmarks.note: Loropéni verified as UNESCO site (2009); Bobo-Dioulasso's historic centre Sya is on the UNESCO tentative list; Sindou Peaks (rock formations near Banfora) are well known but not verified in an opened source.

funFact.value: The name Burkina Faso, adopted in 1984, joins words from two local languages, Mooré and Dyula, and means roughly land of upright, honest people.
funFact.note: Burkina (Mooré, upright/honest) + Faso (Dyula, fatherland); renamed 4 August 1984 under Thomas Sankara. 144 characters.

driveSide.note: RHT per Wikipedia table; matches seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Adopted on 4 August 1984, when Thomas Sankara's revolutionary government renamed Upper Volta as Burkina Faso, the flag replaced a black, white and red one whose stripes stood for the three Volta rivers. Red and green with a yellow star are Pan-African colors drawn from Ethiopia's flag. Red is often said to stand for the revolution, green for farming and natural riches, and the yellow star for the light that guides it.

reasons.feature: Red upper half, green lower half, yellow five-pointed star in the center
reasons.why: Adopted 4 August 1984 with the country's renaming after the 1983 revolution; the constitution (Article 34) describes the red and green flag with a yellow-gold five-pointed star in its center. Designer named by Wikipedia as Ferdinand Dabiré.
Pan-African colors from Ethiopia's flag, chosen to mark a break with the colonial past and unity with other African ex-colonies.

reasons.feature: Meaning of red, green and the star
reasons.why: Red is said to represent the revolution, green the abundance of agricultural and natural riches, and the yellow star the guiding light of the revolution. Wikipedia and FOTW give this reading without attributing it to a law or government statement, so it is presented as the common reading rather than official.
The 1960-1984 flag had black, white and red stripes for the Black, White and Red Volta rivers.

entries.remainingDoubts: Official languages: the amended constitution makes the national languages official collectively but names none, and no implementing law naming specific ones was found in any opened source; the three listed are the principal national languages recognised since 1998, not a legally enumerated list of official languages. If the app needs strict legal accuracy, consider an empty list or a note. Population rounded to 5 s.f. because 3 and 4 s.f. both end in 5. Color meanings downgraded from official to traditional because Wikipedia attributes them to no law or government text. Constitution article number (34) comes from the draft's constituteproject source and was not re-opened. Sindou Peaks not verified in an opened source.

funFact.value: No one lived on the islands until Portuguese sailors arrived in the 1450s; Ribeira Grande, now Cidade Velha, became the first European town in the tropics.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: uninhabited until Portuguese arrival c. 1456; Ribeira Grande founded 1462, the first permanent European settlement in the tropics. 155 characters.

driveSide.note: Infobox drives_on = right; matches seed leftHand=false. The traffic-side list page excerpt was truncated before Cape Verde.

flag.text: Adopted in 1992, this flag replaced a red, yellow and green one with a black star that looked almost like Guinea-Bissau's, as both came from the same independence movement. Pedro Gregório designed it to be mistaken for no other flag. Officially, blue is the sky and sea, the white and red bands are the people's wish for peace and the work of building the nation, and the ten yellow stars are the ten islands, in a circle for unity.

reasons.feature: Five horizontal bands (blue, white, red, white, blue) with a circle of ten yellow stars left of center
reasons.why: Adopted September 1992 (Wikipedia gives 25 September, FOTW 22 September) and defined in the constitution (Article 8 per FOTW) as five unequal horizontal bands in 6:1:1:1:3 proportion with ten five-pointed yellow stars in a circle.

reasons.feature: Meaning of blue, white and red
reasons.why: Cape Verdean government explanation, as reported by Wikipedia: blue is the sky and sea; white and red express the people's desire for peace and their efforts in nation-building.

reasons.feature: Ten yellow stars in a circle
reasons.why: The ten islands of the archipelago, arranged in a circle to symbolise unity (government explanation per Wikipedia).

The 1975 flag used Pan-African red, yellow and green with a black star in the PAIGC style and was nearly identical to Guinea-Bissau's; after the 1991 multi-party election ended one-party rule, architect Pedro Gregório designed a flag that would not be mistaken for another nation's, marking a break with the socialist past.

entries.remainingDoubts: Area taken from the country infobox because the by-area list excerpt did not reach Cape Verde in either fetch (both are expected to read 4,033). Santa Maria Beach not verified in an opened source. Exact adoption day differs between sources (22 September per FOTW vs 25 September 1992 per Wikipedia), so the text gives only the year. Constitution article number (8) comes from FOTW, not re-verified in the constitution itself.

value: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace (Yamoussoukro)
landmarks.note: The Basilica was verified via its Wikipedia article. Taï National Park and Comoé National Park are the country's two UNESCO natural World Heritage sites; they were not opened in a separate page during this session.

funFact.value: The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro, modeled on St. Peter's in Rome, is listed by Guinness World Records as the largest church in the world.
funFact.note: 154 characters. Wikipedia: consecrated 1990 by Pope John Paul II, 30,000 m2 area, 158 m tall, modeled on St. Peter's Basilica, listed by Guinness as the largest church in the world.

driveSide.note: Right-hand traffic, introduced by France in French West Africa; Wikipedia's traffic article lists Ivory Coast among right-hand-traffic countries. Matches the seed (leftHand false).

flag.text: Ivory Coast adopted this flag on 3 December 1959, shortly before independence from France. Presenting it to lawmakers, Minister Jean Delafosse gave the official meaning: orange for the rich, generous land and the struggle of a young people, white for peace, the peace of law, and green for hope and a better future. The three upright bands are often said to follow the layout of the French flag, and it happens to mirror Ireland's flag.

reasons.feature: Orange band next to the flagpole
reasons.why: In his 1959 presentation to the Legislative Assembly, Minister of State Jean Delafosse said orange recalls the color of the country's rich and generous land and the meaning of its struggle, the blood of a young people fighting for emancipation. Re-verified in the Wikipedia flag article during the check pass.
Delafosse's official 1959 explanation: white is peace, but the peace of law (la paix du droit).
Delafosse's official 1959 explanation: green is hope, and for Ivorians the certainty of a better future.

The layout is commonly described as following the model of the French flag of the former colonial power, but the Wikipedia flag article (re-read in the check pass) does not say so: it records only that the French commissioner proposed a red, white and blue design with stars, which Ivorians rejected to keep more distance from France's flag, and that the result resembles Ireland's flag reversed, with 2:3 rather than 1:2 proportions, a resemblance not documented as deliberate. The French-layout clause is therefore hedged.

Adopted by law no. 59-240 of 3 December 1959 by the Ivorian Legislative Assembly, just before the first anniversary of autonomy within the French Community; the flag is defined as orange, white and green in vertical bands of equal size in article 1 of the 1960 constitution, article 29 of the 2000 constitution and article 48 of the 2016 constitution. Law number, date and the three constitution articles re-verified in the Wikipedia flag article.

entries.remainingDoubts: The constitution texts at mjp.univ-perp.fr (1960 and 2016) could not be opened (404 and 503), so the constitutional wording is taken from the Wikipedia flag article and the abidjan.net report of law 59-240. The Wikipedia flag article mentions only the Irish resemblance and the rejected French proposal, not a conscious modeling on the French flag's layout, so that clause stays hedged as a popular reading. The UN population figure was not re-downloaded in the check pass. Taï National Park and Comoé National Park were not verified through a separately opened page. The flag image (ci.png) shows exactly three equal vertical bands, orange, white, green, all covered.

entries.name: Gambia

officialName.note: Per ownerRules and the Wikipedia infobox; the capital T in The is part of the official name.

capital.note: Banjul is the capital; the largest urban area is Serekunda, but it holds no capital role.

population.note: UN World Population Prospects 2024, medium variant, 1 July 2024: 2,759,988 (read directly from the UN WPP2024 CSV). Rounded to 3 significant figures (2,760,000; the value ends in 6, not 5, so the 4-figure exception does not apply). Note the national 2024 census counted 2,422,712, noticeably lower than the UN estimate; the field rule asks for the UN figure.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia's list: 11,295 km2, including about 10,120 km2 of land and 1,180 km2 of water (mostly the Gambia River). The country article rounds this to 11,300 km2.

languages.note: English is the only official language. Mandinka, Pulaar, Wolof, Serer, Jola and others are listed as national or widely spoken languages but not official, so they are excluded by the field rule.

currency.note: Gambian dalasi, ISO code GMD; the usual symbol is D.

landmarks.note: Kunta Kinteh Island (formerly James Island), a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2003, was verified via its Wikipedia article. Arch 22 in Banjul and the Wassu Stone Circles (part of the UNESCO-listed Senegambian stone circles) are well known but were not opened in a separate page during this session.

funFact.value: The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa: a narrow strip along the Gambia River, surrounded by Senegal except for its Atlantic coast.
funFact.note: 146 characters. Wikipedia: the smallest country in continental Africa, elongated along the Gambia River, bounded by Senegal on all sides except its western Atlantic coastline.

driveSide.note: Right, matching the seed. The Gambia changed from left to right on 1 October 1965 to match its French-influenced neighbors (search snippets from worlddata.info and thebftonline.com; Wikipedia's traffic article says former British West Africa has switched to the right). Caution: the automated summary of the Wikipedia The Gambia infobox reported 'Left', which conflicts with every other source and the seed; Right is used.

flag.text: The Gambia raised this flag on 18 February 1965, the day it became independent from Britain. Louis Thomasi designed it, and it was not based on any political party's colors. The colors are usually read as geography: blue in the middle for the Gambia River, which runs the length of the country, red above for the sun and the savanna grassland, and green below for forests and farmland. The thin white lines are said to mean unity and peace.

reasons.why: Said to evoke the sun, because of the country's nearness to the Equator, and the savanna. Reported by Wikipedia (re-read in the check pass) citing Britannica, the CIA World Factbook and DK's Complete Flags of the World; no government text was opened, so it is hedged.
Said to stand for the Gambia River, the country's key geographical feature, which flows through the middle of the country just as the blue band sits in the middle of the flag.
Said to stand for the forest and the agricultural goods on which Gambians heavily depend.
Said to stand for unity and peace.

Adopted on 18 February 1965, the day of independence from Britain, replacing the British Blue Ensign bearing the colony's badge. The winning design was by Pa Louis Thomasi, an accountant; the Wikipedia article calls it the winning design but does not describe a formal competition, so the earlier 'competition entry' wording was dropped. Wikipedia notes the flag has no political basis and is one of the few African flags not using the colors of the leading political party. It stayed unchanged through the 1982-1989 Senegambia confederation with Senegal.

entries.remainingDoubts: No Gambian government or flag-law text was opened: the Britannica flag pages returned 404, 503 and 403 and the CIA World Factbook flag page now redirects to a notice that the Factbook has been discontinued, so the color meanings rest on the Wikipedia flag article and the Britannica, CIA and DK references it cites, and are labeled traditional rather than official. Whether a formal design competition was held is not stated in the Wikipedia flag article. The automated summary of the Wikipedia country infobox reported driving on the left, which contradicts the 1965 switch to the right and the seed; Right is used. The UN population figure was not re-downloaded in the check pass. Arch 22 and the Wassu Stone Circles were not verified through a separately opened page. The flag image (gm.png) shows red, thin white, blue, thin white, green horizontal bands, all covered.

entries.name: Ghana

capital.note: Accra is both capital and largest city, as the ownerRules require.

population.note: UN World Population Prospects 2024, medium variant, 1 July 2024: 34,427,414 (read directly from the UN WPP2024 CSV). Rounded to 3 significant figures. Not re-downloaded in the verification pass; the rounding was checked.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia's list: 238,537 km2, including about 227,533 km2 of land and 11,000 km2 of water (largely Lake Volta). The country article infobox gives a slightly different rounded figure (about 240,000 km2); the list figure is used as the field rule requires.

languages.note: English is the sole official language, as the ownerRules state. Twi, Fante, Ewe, Ga, Dagbani and others are government-sponsored languages, not official, so they are excluded.

currency.note: Ghanaian cedi, ISO code GHS; the symbol GH₵ is the one in general use.

landmarks.note: Lake Volta (behind the Akosombo Dam) is described in the Ghana article. Cape Coast Castle (a UNESCO-listed former slave fort) and Kakum National Park (famous for its rainforest canopy walkway) are well known but were not opened in a separate page during this session.

funFact.value: Lake Volta, formed when the Akosombo Dam was completed in 1965, is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world by surface area.
funFact.note: 132 characters. Wikipedia describes Lake Volta as the world's largest reservoir by surface area and third largest by volume; the fact is phrased as 'one of the largest' so it stays true even if rankings are revised.

driveSide.note: Right, matching the seed. Ghana switched from left to right on 4 August 1974 under the Operation Keep Right campaign (search snippets from graphiconline.com and citinewsroom.com; Wikipedia's traffic article says former British West Africa has switched to the right).

flag.text: Ghana adopted this flag at independence from Britain on 6 March 1957. Designer Theodosia Okoh explained: red remembers those who died or worked for independence, gold is the mineral wealth that gave the Gold Coast its name, and green is its rich forests. The black star, a sign of African freedom and unity, comes from Marcus Garvey's Black Star Line shipping company. Red, gold and green are Pan-African colors, first used by Ethiopia.

reasons.why: The designer, Theodosia Okoh, said red commemorates those who died or worked for the country's independence from British rule. The Flag of Ghana article (re-read in the check pass) gives the same meaning in summary form; the direct quotation is in the Theodosia Okoh article.
Okoh said gold was influenced by the mineral-rich nature of the land; the colonial territory was called the Gold Coast after its gold deposits. Britannica summarizes it as the wealth of the country.
Okoh chose green because Ghana lies in the tropics and is blessed with rich vegetation; it is read as the forests and natural wealth, including crops such as cocoa.

reasons.feature: Black five-pointed star in the center
reasons.why: Okoh said the lone star is symbolic of African emancipation and unity in the struggle against colonialism; Britannica calls it the lodestar of African freedom. Its origin is documented as the flag of the Black Star Line, the shipping line incorporated by Marcus Garvey, which operated from 1919 to 1922 (re-verified in the Flag of Ghana article), and whose Pan-African ideas influenced Kwame Nkrumah.

These are the Pan-African colors derived from the flag of Ethiopia; Wikipedia says Ghana's was the second African flag, after the Ethiopian Empire's, to use red, gold and green, in inverted order, and many later African flags followed.

Adopted on 6 March 1957 at independence. After the 1964 constitutional referendum the gold band was replaced by white to match the colors of Nkrumah's Convention People's Party; the original 1957 design was restored in February 1966 after his overthrow in a coup. Dates re-verified in the Flag of Ghana article.

entries.remainingDoubts: No Ghanaian government page was reachable (the Ghana Embassy Berlin page redirected and did not render), so the color meanings rest on the designer's own quoted statement in the Theodosia Okoh Wikipedia article plus the Flag of Ghana article and Britannica, which is why they are labeled official (designer) rather than cited to a law; the Flag of Ghana article itself gives the meanings only in summary, not as a direct Okoh quotation, and the Okoh article was not re-opened in the check pass. Wikipedia's area list (238,537 km2) differs from the country infobox (about 240,000 km2); the list value is used. The UN population figure was not re-downloaded in the check pass. Cape Coast Castle and Kakum National Park were not verified through a separately opened page. The flag image (gh.png) shows red, gold and green horizontal bands with a black five-pointed star centered on the gold band, all covered.

entries.name: Guinea

capital.note: Per seed ownerRules and Wikipedia infobox; single capital.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, medium variant, mid-2024 estimate 14,754,785 as reproduced on Worldometers (page states it elaborates UN WPP 2024 data); rounded to 3 significant figures. The UN data-portal API returned HTTP 401, so the figure was not read from the UN site directly. Cross-check: Wikipedia's UN table (WPP 2024) gives 14,405,465 for 1 July 2023, consistent with 14.75 million in 2024. Rounding re-checked by the reviewer.

areaSqKm.note: Total area including inland water: 245,717 km2 land plus 140 km2 water (0.1 percent water), per Wikipedia's list (which cites the CIA World Factbook).

languages.note: French is the official language, per seed ownerRules (binding). Wikipedia's infobox additionally lists national languages (Susu, Fulani, Malinke, Kissi, Kpelle, Toma and others); these are not included here.

currency.note: ISO code GNF; Wikipedia gives the abbreviation FG (also Fr or GFr). Sole legal tender; reintroduced in 1985 after the syli.

landmarks.note: Mount Nimba (1,752 m) is Guinea's highest point and a UNESCO nature reserve, though its summit sits on the border with Côte d'Ivoire; Fouta Djallon is the central highland region; the Îles de Los lie about 2 km off Conakry and are known for beaches.

funFact.value: The Niger River rises in Guinea's highlands only about 240 km from the Atlantic, yet runs 4,180 km through Mali and Niger before reaching the sea in Nigeria.
funFact.note: 157 characters (re-counted). Source location (Guinea Highlands, about 240 km from the Atlantic), length (about 4,180 km) and the course through Mali and Niger to Nigeria are from the Niger River article; the Guinea article confirms the country holds the headwaters of the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers.

driveSide.note: Right, matching the seed (leftHand false). WorldStandards lists Guinea as right-hand traffic; the Wikipedia traffic article notes all former French colonies drive on the right. No source disagreed.

flag.text: Guinea adopted this flag on 10 November 1958, weeks after leaving French rule. The upright bands follow the French flag's layout, but the colors are the Pan-African red, yellow and green, taken from Ghana's 1957 flag. President Sékou Touré said red stands for the blood of those who died fighting colonial rule and for work, yellow for gold and the sun, and green for the land's plants, matching the motto Work, Justice, Solidarity.

reasons.feature: Three upright bands of equal width
reasons.why: The layout copies the vertical design of the French flag, the former colonial power; the flag was adopted on 10 November 1958 with the publication of Guinea's first constitution, weeks after independence from France on 2 October 1958.

reasons.feature: Red, yellow and green color set
reasons.why: These are the Pan-African colors. Wikipedia's flag article says they were adapted from the colors of the Rassemblement Démocratique Africain (RDA), the dominant movement at independence (Sékou Touré led its Guinean section), and that the RDA in turn took them from the flag of Ghana, which first adopted them in 1957.
According to first president Sékou Touré, red symbolizes the blood of the anti-colonialist martyrs and the labor of the working classes.
According to Sékou Touré, yellow represents Guinean gold as well as the sun.
According to Sékou Touré, green represents the country's vegetation and the continued prosperity arising from its natural resources.

reasons.feature: Order of the colors and the national motto
reasons.why: The symbolism of the three colors is matched, in order, to the three parts of the national motto Travail, Justice, Solidarité (Work, Justice, Solidarity).

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of UN WPP 2024 (the UN data-portal API refused the request with HTTP 401); the figure matches the WPP 2023 trend but was not read from a UN page. The color meanings are attributed to Sékou Touré by the Wikipedia flag article (confirmed on this pass); the primary speech and the constitution text (which only names the colors) were not opened. The draft's claim that the Democratic Party of Guinea used the colors from 1954 was not supported by the article, which credits the RDA, so it was replaced. Wikipedia's Guinea infobox lists several national languages alongside French; only French is given per the seed's ownerRules. Mount Nimba's summit lies on the border with Côte d'Ivoire, so a reviewer may prefer a landmark wholly inside Guinea (for example Kinkon Falls near Pita).

entries.name: Guinea-Bissau

capital.note: Per seed ownerRules and Wikipedia infobox; single capital.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, medium variant, mid-2024 estimate 2,201,352 as reproduced on Worldometers (page states it elaborates UN WPP 2024 data); rounded to 3 significant figures. UN data-portal API was not accessible (HTTP 401). Cross-check: Wikipedia's UN table (WPP 2024) gives 2,153,339 for 1 July 2023, consistent with 2.20 million in 2024.

areaSqKm.note: Total area including inland water: 28,120 km2 land plus 8,010 km2 water (about 22 percent water, reflecting the many estuaries and islands), per Wikipedia's list.

languages.note: Portuguese is the sole official language, per seed ownerRules (binding) and the Wikipedia infobox. Guinea-Bissau Creole is listed by Wikipedia as a national language and lingua franca but is not official, so it is omitted.

currency.note: ISO code XOF; exact wording required by the field rules. Wikipedia infobox lists the West African CFA franc as the currency.

landmarks.note: Bijagós Archipelago: 88 islands and islets with a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve; Orango Islands National Park within it is known for saltwater hippos; Amura Fort (Fortaleza de São José da Amura, built 1753) in Bissau holds Amílcar Cabral's mausoleum. Wikipedia gives the English name as Fort São José of Amura, locally Amura Fort.

funFact.value: The Bijagós Archipelago off Guinea-Bissau's coast has 88 islands and islets and is home to rare saltwater hippos that swim in the sea between them.
funFact.note: 147 characters (re-counted). Wikipedia's Guinea-Bissau article states the archipelago comprises 88 islands and islets and that Orango Island is home to rare saltwater hippopotamuses.

driveSide.note: Right, matching the seed (leftHand false). Both the Wikipedia infobox and WorldStandards list right-hand traffic; no source disagreed.

flag.text: Adopted on 24 September 1973, when Guinea-Bissau declared independence from Portugal, the flag copies the 1961 flag of the PAIGC independence party, itself modeled on Ghana's flag and its Pan-African colors. The black star, also from Ghana, is often said to stand for Africa's people and the party's leadership. No law gives the colors a meaning; many read red as blood shed for freedom, yellow as sun and savanna, green as forests and hope.

reasons.feature: Overall design: red upright band at the flagpole side, yellow over green on the right
reasons.why: Adopted 24 September 1973 at the declaration of independence from Portugal; it is almost identical to the flag the PAIGC (the independence party) adopted in 1961, which carried the party's initials under the star and drew on the flags of neighboring Ghana and Guinea.

reasons.feature: Red, yellow and green color set
reasons.why: These are the Pan-African colors, popularized by Ghana's 1957 flag and before that by Ethiopia's flag, and shared with many African flags.

It is the Black Star of Africa taken from Ghana's flag; Wikipedia says it symbolizes the leadership of the PAIGC, with its black color standing for the people of Africa. This reading is not set out in law.
Popularly read as the blood shed during the independence struggle (the revolution).
Popularly read as the northern savannas and agriculture; some sources instead say the sun or mineral wealth.
Popularly read as the southern forests and agriculture, and as hope.

The 1975 government gazette description and the later constitutional text only describe the positions of the colors and the star (without even fixing shades or ratio) and give them no symbolism, so all color meanings above are popular interpretations.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of UN WPP 2024 (the UN data-portal API refused the request with HTTP 401). The traditional color meanings differ between sources (yellow as savanna, sun or minerals), and none is official, as the text says. The draft's reference to a Ghana-Guinea union of 1958 was not supported by the flag article and was removed. The English name for the Bissau fortress varies (Fort São José of Amura, Amura Fort, Fortaleza da Amura); the plain local English form is used. The flag's exact 1:2 proportion is not mentioned in the text.

entries.name: Liberia

capital.note: Per seed ownerRules; Wikipedia confirms Monrovia as the capital and largest city.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, medium variant, mid-2024 estimate 5,612,817 as reproduced on Worldometers (page states it elaborates UN WPP 2024 data); rounded to 3 significant figures. UN data-portal API was not accessible (HTTP 401). Cross-check: Wikipedia's UN table (WPP 2024) gives 5,493,031 for 1 July 2023, consistent with 5.61 million in 2024.

areaSqKm.note: Total area including inland water: 96,320 km2 land plus 15,049 km2 water (13.5 percent water), per Wikipedia's list (which cites the CIA World Factbook). The Liberia article infobox rounds this to 111,370 km2.

languages.note: English is the sole official language, per seed ownerRules (binding) and the Wikipedia infobox; the many indigenous languages are not official.

currency.note: critic: The other three dual-legal-tender entries in this batch (ZW, LS, NA) join the two currencies with ', '; Liberia alone uses ' and '.

landmarks.note: Sapo National Park is the country's largest rainforest reserve; Providence Island in Monrovia is where the 1822 settlers landed; Kpatawee Waterfall is a well-known natural sight in Bong County. Mount Nimba was avoided because it is already used for Guinea and is shared by three countries.

funFact.value: Liberia's capital Monrovia was founded in 1822 by settlers from the United States and renamed in 1824 after James Monroe, the US president at the time.
funFact.note: 151 characters (re-counted). Wikipedia's Monrovia article: settlement established in 1822 by the American Colonization Society's settlers (free people of color from the United States), first called Christopolis, renamed Monrovia in 1824 after President James Monroe.

driveSide.note: Right, matching the seed (leftHand false). Both the Wikipedia infobox and WorldStandards list right-hand traffic; no source disagreed.

flag.text: Liberia's flag dates from 24 August 1847 and was sewn by a committee of seven women. It resembles the US flag because Liberia was founded in 1822 as a settlement for free Black Americans. The eleven stripes are said to stand for the eleven signers of the Declaration of Independence, the white star for Africa's first republic, and the blue square for Africa. A 1961 law reads blue as liberty and justice, white as purity, red as courage.

reasons.feature: Overall design resembling the United States flag (stripes with a blue square and star in the upper left corner)
reasons.why: Liberia was founded from 1822 by free people of color and formerly enslaved people from the United States and the Caribbean, with the support of the US government and the American Colonization Society; the flag was adopted on 24 August 1847, a month after the 26 July 1847 declaration of independence.

reasons.feature: Committee of seven women who designed and sewed the flag
reasons.why: At the request of Governor Joseph Jenkins Roberts, a committee headed by Susannah Elizabeth Lewis, with Matilda Newport, Rachel Johnson, Mary Hunter, Sarah McGill Russwurm, Colonette Teage Ellis and Sara Draper, designed and hand-stitched the first flag in 1847.

reasons.feature: Eleven horizontal red and white stripes
reasons.why: Widely said to represent the eleven signers of the Liberian Declaration of Independence, with red and white together read as courage and moral excellence. The 11 April 1961 flag law (section 30) describes the stripes but gives them no meaning; Flags of the World attributes this reading to later writers, so it is given as the customary reading.
Commonly said to mark Liberia as the first independent republic on the African continent; not a meaning given in the 1961 law.

reasons.feature: Blue square in the upper left corner
reasons.why: Commonly said to represent the African continent; the 11 April 1961 law specifies a square blue area reaching down to the bottom of the third red stripe but assigns it no meaning.

Section 31 of the Flag Law approved by the National Legislature on 11 April 1961 defines the colors: blue symbolizes liberty, justice and fidelity; white purity, cleanliness and guilelessness; red steadfastness, valor and fervor (the text's 'courage' paraphrases valor).

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of UN WPP 2024 (the UN data-portal API refused the request with HTTP 401). The claim that the Central Bank of Liberia Act 1999, section 19.2, makes the US dollar legal tender appeared only in a search snippet; the article opened confirms both currencies are legal tender but does not cite that section. The 1961-law color meanings were confirmed on Flags of the World (section 31 of the 11 April 1961 Flag Law), not from the law text itself; Wikipedia's flag article confirms the 1961 law describes construction without color symbolism beyond that. The stripes, star and square meanings are widely published but not in the law, so they are marked traditional. Area differs by 1 km2 between Wikipedia's list (111,369) and the country infobox (111,370); the list value is used.

entries.name: Mali

capital.note: Single capital; matches seed ownerRules; infobox re-confirmed.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, 1 July 2024 estimate 24,478,595 (read from Worldometers, which states it reproduces WPP 2024 medium variant; the UN data-portal API returned 401). Rounded to 4 significant figures because 3 would give 24,500,000 (ends in 5 then zeros). Wikipedia's UN list (WPP 2024) shows 23,769,127 for mid-2023, consistent with this.

areaSqKm.note: Total area (land plus inland water): 1,220,190 km2 land plus about 20,000 km2 inland water.

languages.note: Article 31 of the 2023 constitution (promulgated 22 July 2023) reads 'Les langues nationales sont les langues officielles du Mali' and 'Le francais est la langue de travail'. The constitution does not name the languages; the 13 national languages are those of Law 96-049 (1996). Spellings follow the Wikipedia Mali infobox as re-read in review (Bambara, Bobo, Bozo, Dogon, Fula, Hassaniya Arabic, Kassonke, Maninke, Minyanka, Senufo, Songhay, Soninke, Tamasheq); the review changed the draft's 'Khassonke' and 'Maninka' to the infobox forms. French is only a working language (the infobox labels it a de facto working language), so it is not listed.

currency.note: XOF; Wikipedia infobox re-confirmed 'West African CFA franc (XOF)' in review. Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso announced in 2024 that they intend to leave the CFA zone, but the draft's search (reports dated March 2026) found the CFA franc still in use and no replacement in circulation.

landmarks.note: Great Mosque of Djenné and Timbuktu confirmed from the opened pages (both UNESCO sites). Bandiagara Escarpment (Land of the Dogons, UNESCO) is from general knowledge; its page was not opened within the call budget.

funFact.value: The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world, and the whole town replasters it by hand in a festival every year.
funFact.note: 141 characters. Wikipedia: largest adobe (mud-brick) building in the world; current building 1907; annual communal replastering.

driveSide.note: Matches seed leftHand=false; article states France introduced right-hand traffic in French West Africa including Mali.

flag.text: Mali's green, gold and red bands are the Pan-African colors also seen on the flags of Ghana, Guinea and Senegal. Mali took them up in 1959 while briefly united with Senegal; that flag had a black human figure, the kanaga, in the center. It was removed in March 1961 because many Muslims objected to a human image. Green is often said to stand for fertile land, gold for mineral wealth and red for blood shed for independence.

reasons.feature: Three upright bands of green, gold and red
reasons.why: These are the Pan-African colors, taken up after World War II by the African Democratic Rally and drawn from the flags of Ethiopia and Ghana; Mali first adopted them on 4 April 1959 as the flag of the Mali Federation with Senegal, and kept them at independence. Image at /tmp/flagwork/out/ml.png shows exactly these three plain vertical bands.

The 1959 federation flag carried a black kanaga, a stylized human figure with raised arms from Dogon culture. It was removed on 1 March 1961 after Muslim objections to depicting a human figure, leaving the plain three-band flag used today.

Green for the fertility of the land, gold for purity and mineral wealth, red for the blood shed for independence. These readings come from secondary sources (WorldAtlas cited by Wikipedia); no official Malian statement assigning meanings was found, so the text hedges them with 'often said to'.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal itself (API returned 401). The 13-language list follows Law 96-049 as reported by Wikipedia; the constitution does not enumerate them, and English spellings vary between sources (review adopted the Wikipedia infobox forms Kassonke and Maninke). Bandiagara Escarpment page not opened. CFA franc status checked only via search-result snippets dated March 2026. Whether any Malian text officially assigns meanings to the colors was not verified; the flag text treats the meanings as popular readings.

entries.name: Mauritania

capital.note: Single capital; matches seed ownerRules.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, 1 July 2024 estimate 5,169,395 (read from Worldometers, which states it reproduces WPP 2024 medium variant; UN data-portal API returned 401). Rounded to 3 significant figures. Wikipedia's UN list shows 5,022,441 for mid-2023, consistent.

areaSqKm.note: Total area; the list gives 1,030,700 km2 land and 0 km2 inland water.

languages.note: Hand edit after the workflow: Article 6 of the constitution makes Arabic the official language and names Arabic, Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof as national languages; the catalog lists national languages where the constitution enumerates them (as for Congo, DR Congo, Botswana and Malawi). Article 6 of the constitution: Arabic is the official language; Arabic, Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof are national languages. Only the official language is listed, per seed ownerRules and field rules.

currency.note: Symbol UM, ISO code MRU (since the 1:10 redenomination of 1 January 2018).

landmarks.note: Richat Structure confirmed from its page (near Ouadane, Adrar Region). Banc d'Arguin National Park and Chinguetti (both UNESCO sites) are from general knowledge; their pages were not opened within the call budget.

funFact.value: The Richat Structure near Ouadane, nicknamed the Eye of Africa, is an eroded rock dome about 40 km across that is easy to spot from space.
funFact.note: 138 characters. Wikipedia: 40 km diameter, eroded geological dome (not an impact crater), landmark for astronauts; the page also calls it Eye of the Sahara.

driveSide.note: Matches seed leftHand=false; article lists Mauritania among former French territories using right-hand traffic.

flag.text: The green center with a gold crescent and star dates from 1959, just before independence from France. Green and the crescent and star are old symbols of Islam, the religion of nearly all Mauritanians; gold is often linked to the Sahara sands that cover most of the land. The red bands at the top and bottom were added after a 2017 referendum; the government said they honor the blood of Mauritanians who fought French colonial rule.

reasons.feature: Green background with gold crescent and star
reasons.why: Adopted 1 April 1959 when Mauritania became an autonomous republic, replacing the French flag, and kept at independence on 28 November 1960 (date re-confirmed on the Wikipedia flag page in review). Wikipedia: the star and crescent, as well as the color green, are symbols of Islam; the country is an Islamic republic. Green and gold are also Pan-African colors.

reasons.feature: Gold color of crescent and star
reasons.why: Popularly linked to the sands of the Sahara, which covers about 90 percent of the country. The Wikipedia flag page gives gold only as the specified color of the Islamic symbols and states no separate meaning for it, so this is a common reading rather than an official one and the text hedges it with 'often linked to'.

reasons.feature: Two red bands at top and bottom
reasons.why: Added in 2017 (re-confirmed in review): over 86 percent of voters approved the change in the referendum of 5 August 2017 (54 percent turnout); the National Assembly adopted Bill No. 136/17 on 12 October 2017; Decree No. 2017-467 of 25 October 2017 fixed the new flag; first raised on independence day, 28 November 2017. Red officially stands for the blood shed by Mauritanians who fought for the country's independence from France. Image at /tmp/flagwork/out/mr.png shows the two red bands, green center, gold crescent and star, all covered in the text.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 (UN API returned 401). The 2017 sequence (referendum 5 August, Assembly bill 12 October, decree 25 October, first raised 28 November) is now confirmed from the Wikipedia flag page; the text avoids naming any single adoption date. The 'gold = Sahara sands' reading is not stated on the flag page and remains labeled traditional. Banc d'Arguin and Chinguetti pages not opened.

officialName.note: Wikipedia infobox form, with 'the'; re-confirmed in review.

capital.note: Single capital; matches seed ownerRules; infobox re-confirmed.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, 1 July 2024 estimate 27,032,412 (read from Worldometers, which states it reproduces WPP 2024 medium variant; UN data-portal API returned 401). Rounded to 3 significant figures. Wikipedia's UN list shows 26,159,867 for mid-2023, consistent.

areaSqKm.note: Total area (land plus inland water): 1,266,700 km2 land plus 300 km2 inland water.

languages.note: The Refoundation (transitional) Charter adopted after the February 2025 national assemblies and published in the Journal officiel on 31 March 2025 makes Hausa the national language and demotes French to a working language alongside English (press reports cite article 12). Re-checked in review: the Wikipedia Niger infobox lists Hausa as the official language ('the official and national language') and English and French as working languages 'as per the 2025 transitional charter'. Hausa alone is listed; working languages are excluded under the field rules. flag.text: Niger chose its flag in 1959, a year before independence from France: orange, white and green bands with an orange circle in the middle. They are commonly read as the land from north to south: orange for the Sahara desert, white for the dry grassland between, green for the fertile south along the Niger River. The circle is usually said to be the sun.

flag.text: Senegal adopted this flag in 1960 on leaving the short-lived Mali Federation. flag.text: Barthélemy Boganda, its first leader, designed the flag, adopted on 1 December 1958. reasons.feature: Overall design: four horizontal bands with a vertical red stripe

flag.text: The blue flag with a star dates from 1877, when Belgium's King Leopold II used it for his African association; the star meant light for Africa. A red diagonal stripe edged in yellow was added in 1963, and after the Zaire flag years this design returned in the 2006 constitution with a lighter sky blue. Blue is said to mean peace, red the blood of the nation's martyrs, yellow its wealth and the star a bright future, though no law fixes them.

reasons.feature: Blue background with a yellow star in the upper left corner
reasons.why: The blue flag with a gold star was created in 1877 for King Leopold II's International African Association and kept by the Congo Free State and Belgian Congo; the star was meant to symbolize a bright light shining on the continent.

reasons.feature: Red diagonal stripe with thin yellow edges
reasons.why: Introduced in 1963, three years after independence, replacing the six small stars of the 1960 flag when the provinces changed; kept in the 1966 version and restored in 1997 and 2006.

reasons.feature: Adoption in 2006 with a lighter sky blue
reasons.why: Article 1 of the 2006 constitution describes a sky-blue flag with a yellow star in the upper left corner crossed diagonally by a red band finely outlined in yellow; it took effect 18 February 2006 after the green Zaire flag of 1971-1997.

reasons.feature: Meanings: blue peace, red blood of martyrs, yellow wealth, star a radiant future
reasons.why: Widely reported explanation (Wikipedia attributes it to the 2006 constitution, but the constitutional text only describes the design; CRW Flags traces the wording to a press report), so it is presented as what is said rather than law.

entries.remainingDoubts: The color meanings are commonly attributed to the 2006 constitution, but Article 1 only describes the flag; no official decree giving the meanings was found, so they are labeled traditional. Mount Nyiragongo was not verified on a dedicated page. Population figures for the DRC vary widely between sources; the UN WPP 2024 value (via Worldometers) is used. flag.text: Adopted at independence from Spain in 1968: three bands of green, white and red with a blue triangle at the pole side. Green is said to stand for forests, white for peace, red for blood shed for freedom and blue for the sea joining mainland and islands. The seal shows a silk-cotton tree, where tradition says the first treaty with Spain was signed, six stars for the mainland and five main islands, and the motto Unity, Peace, Justice.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands of green, white and red with a blue triangle at the flagpole side
reasons.why: The constitution (Art. 4.2) prescribes exactly this layout: green, white and red in three equal horizontal stripes and a blue triangle at the end nearest the flagpole. Confirmed against the flag image /tmp/flagwork/out/gq.png.

The flag was raised on 12 October 1968, the day of independence from Spain; the coat of arms was changed under Macías Nguema from 1978 and the original restored on 21 August 1979 when he was overthrown (Wikipedia flag article, re-read in the check pass).
Said (Whitney Smith, Britannica) to stand for the vegetation on which most people rely; no law assigns the meaning, so the text hedges with 'is said to'.
Said to stand for peace (Britannica/Wikipedia); not defined in law.
Said to stand for the blood shed by those who fought for independence (Britannica/Wikipedia); not defined in law.
Said to stand for the sea that links the mainland with the islands (Britannica/Wikipedia); not defined in law.

reasons.feature: Silk-cotton tree in the central seal

reasons.feature: Six gold six-pointed stars above the seal

flag.text: Gabon's flag has three equal bands of green, yellow and blue. The 1959 flag, used while Gabon was still linked to France, had a narrower yellow band and a small French flag in the upper left corner; both changed just before independence in 1960. The constitution gives the colors no meaning. Green is often read as the rainforests covering most of the land, yellow as the sun and the equator that crosses Gabon, and blue as the Atlantic coast.

reasons.feature: Three equal horizontal bands of green, yellow and blue

reasons.feature: 1959 version with narrower yellow band and French flag in the upper left corner, changed 1960

Wikipedia gives 9 August 1960 as the adoption date, a week before independence on 17 August 1960.
Commonly read (Britannica, CIA Factbook via Wikipedia) as the extensive forests, a key economic resource; not assigned in law, so the text says 'often read as'.
Commonly read as the sun and the equator that runs through the country; interpretive, not legal.
Commonly read as the South Atlantic Ocean along Gabon's long coast; interpretive, not legal.

Shared Pan-African origin named in the text.

flag.text: At independence in 1962 the flag had its white diagonal cross and circle, holding a royal drum and a sorghum plant. The drum went when the monarchy fell in 1966, and in 1967 three red six-pointed stars replaced the sorghum. They match the motto Unity, Work, Progress and are often read as the Hutu, Tutsi and Twa peoples. White is said to mean peace, red the independence struggle and green hope. The constitution gives the colors no meaning.

reasons.feature: White diagonal cross and central white circle
reasons.why: Present since the first independence flag, authorized by the king in March 1962 and hoisted on 1 July 1962, when the circle held the sacred royal drum (karyenda) and a sorghum plant. After the monarchy was abolished in November 1966 the drum was removed; the sorghum plant stayed until the stars replaced it in 1967.

reasons.feature: Three red six-pointed stars with green edges
reasons.why: Introduced in the design that became official on 28 June 1967 (Wikipedia and Britannica), after the monarchy was overthrown in 1966; they correspond to the national motto Unity, Work, Progress (Ubumwe, Ibikorwa, Amajambere).

reasons.feature: Three stars as the three peoples
reasons.why: Commonly also read as the Hutu, Tutsi and Twa; an older reading was loyalty to God, king and country. Britannica presents the ethnic reading as likely rather than fixed; Wikipedia lists all three readings.
Said to symbolize peace.
Said to symbolize the independence struggle and the suffering of the nation.
Said to symbolize hope placed in future development.

The constitution (Article 8 per Flags of the World) names the three colors green, white and red, the diagonal cross, the white disc and the three six-pointed stars, but gives no meaning (Wikipedia: the colors are defined in the constitution as simply green, white and red); proportions were set at 3:5 by decree on 27 September 1982.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population: WPP 2024 mid-2024 value taken from Worldometers' table citing WPP 2024 (14,047,786) because the UN list page on Wikipedia still shows only 2022/2023 columns; Wikipedia's country infobox shows 14,151,540 for 2024 from another source. Flag history: Britannica and Wikipedia agree the 1962 flag held a drum and a sorghum plant and that the drum went after the monarchy's fall in November 1966, with the stars adopted 28 June 1967; Wikipedia's wording about the 1966-67 interim flag is loose, so the text says only that the stars replaced the sorghum in 1967. Flag color meanings are documented by Britannica, Wikipedia and Flags of the World but are not in the constitution, so they are presented as what is said rather than law; no designer is credited. Wikipedia notes Burundi has considered switching to left-hand traffic, but right-hand traffic remains in force.

driveSide.note: Right-hand traffic per Wikipedia's country table (French colony before 1975), matching the seed's leftHand=false.

flag.text: The flag was adopted in 2001. Its four stripes and four stars stand for the four islands, including French-run Mayotte, which Comoros claims. Yellow is usually read as Mohéli, white as Mayotte, red as Anjouan and blue as Grande Comore, though the constitution gives no meanings. The white crescent and four stars have been on every Comorian flag since 1963, and with the green triangle they are read as symbols of Islam.

reasons.feature: Four horizontal stripes: yellow, white, red, blue
reasons.why: Introduced with the 2001 constitution and widely explained as the four islands of the archipelago; the usual matching (yellow Mohéli, white Mayotte, red Anjouan, blue Grande Comore) is an interpretation recorded by Flags of the World and Wikipedia, not stated in the constitution (Wikipedia: the colors are defined in the constitution as simply yellow, white, red, blue and green).

The four islands Grande Comore, Mohéli, Anjouan and Mayotte; the crescent-and-four-stars motif dates from the 1963 flag drawn by French heraldist Suzanne Gauthier and has been kept on every later flag (1975, 1978, 1992, 1996, 2001). Mayotte voted to stay French in 1974-75 and is claimed by Comoros.

Green and the crescent are read as symbols of Islam, the religion of most Comorians; Flags of the World also records the green triangle as standing for the federation of islands. The triangle shape itself is new in the 2001 design (earlier flags were all green).

Became official with the constitution promulgated 23 December 2001 (Wikipedia gives 23 December 2001 as the adoption date; Flags of the World says hoisted 31 December 2001); the 2018 constitution (Article 9 in the Constitute Project text) describes four equal stripes yellow, white, red and blue, a green isosceles triangle at the pole, a white crescent and four white stars, and assigns no meanings.

entries.remainingDoubts: The stripe-to-island mapping is an interpretation (Flags of the World attributes it to Jaume Ollé, 2001) and is not in the constitution; the text says 'usually read as'. Area differs between Wikipedia's area list (1,861 km2, used, not re-read in the verification pass) and the country infobox (1,659 km2 when read); the UN figure of 2,235 km2 includes Mayotte. Population uses WPP 2024 via Worldometers (866,628); the national figure shown in Wikipedia's infobox is higher. Wikipedia's infobox credits Suzanne Gauthier as designer of the current flag; Britannica says she designed the 1963 flag whose crescent and stars the current flag keeps, so the text does not name a designer for the 2001 layout. The article number for the flag clause in the 2018 constitution was taken from the draft and not re-verified.

flag.text: Djibouti raised this flag on 27 June 1977, the day it gained independence from France, using the design of an earlier independence movement's flag. Light blue is traditionally said to mean the sky, the sea and the Issa, a Somali people, and echoes Somalia's flag. Green is linked to the land and the Afar people. The white triangle is said to mean peace and the red star unity. The constitution gives the colors no official meaning.

reasons.why: Officially hoisted on 27 June 1977 at independence from France; the layout and colors come from the flag of the independence movement. Wikipedia says the Front de Libération de la Côte des Somalis (FLCS) created it as its flag in the 1960s with support from the Ligue Populaire Africaine pour l'Indépendance (LPAI); Britannica names the LPAI; Flags of the World says the design was in use from 1972 and credits Mahamoud Harbi. Because the sources disagree on the decade, the text gives no date for the movement.
Said to stand for the sky and the sea and for the Issa, a Somali people; it echoes the light blue of Somalia's flag.
Said to stand for the everlasting green of the earth (Britannica: prosperity) and for the Afar people.

reasons.feature: White triangle at the pole side
reasons.why: Said to stand for peace (Britannica also gives equality).
Said to stand for unity and, per Wikipedia, for the blood shed by those who died for independence and for Djibouti as one of the five regions inhabited by Somali people.

The constitution's opening articles (Constitute Project text of the 1992 constitution as amended in 2010) define the emblem as the blue, green and white flag bearing a red five-pointed star, and give no meanings; Wikipedia notes the popular meanings echo the national anthem.

entries.remainingDoubts: Sources disagree on which independence movement's flag the design came from and when (FLCS in the 1960s with LPAI support per Wikipedia, LPAI per Britannica, in use since 1972 and designed by Mahamoud Harbi per Flags of the World), so the text names no movement or date. Color meanings are popular readings echoing the national anthem, not law; the exact article number of the constitution's emblem clause (Article 1 or 2 depending on the edition) was not re-verified, so the reason says 'opening articles'. Population uses WPP 2024 (1,168,722, via Worldometers citing WPP 2024) rather than the 2024 census count of 1,066,809.

languages.note: Eritrea has no official language in law: the 1997 constitution (Article 4) only says the equality of all Eritrean languages is guaranteed. funFact.value: Eritrea takes its name from the ancient Greek name for the Red Sea, the Erythraean Sea, which forms the country's entire coastline.
funFact.note: Etymology per the Wikipedia article lead; Eritrea's whole coast lies on the Red Sea. 131 characters.

flag.text: Adopted at independence in 1993 and standardized in 1995, the flag copies the red, green and blue triangles of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front flag of 1977. Red is officially for blood shed for independence, green for farming and herds, blue for the sea's wealth. The gold olive branch and wreath replaced the front's star and come from Eritrea's 1952 flag, which honored the United Nations. The 30 leaves are said to mark 30 years of war.

reasons.feature: Red triangle from the pole, green above, blue below
reasons.why: Layout and colors copied from the Eritrean People's Liberation Front flag of 1977; first hoisted as the national flag on 24 May 1993 and standardized on 5 December 1995 (leaf count fixed, proportions changed from 2:3 to 1:2). The constitution (Article 4) names green, red and blue with golden olive leaves but gives no meanings.
The government's interpretation, as reported by Wikipedia, is that red stands for the blood shed in the struggle for independence; Britannica traces the same reading to the EPLF.
Government interpretation: green stands for the agriculture and livestock of the country.
Government interpretation: blue stands for the bounty of the sea (the Red Sea).

reasons.feature: Gold olive branch inside a wreath
reasons.why: In 1993 it replaced the yellow star of the EPLF flag; the vertical olive branch encircled by an olive wreath is derived from Eritrea's 1952 to 1962 federation flag, whose light blue background honored the United Nations.

Fixed at 30 when the flag was standardized in 1995; Wikipedia and Britannica say they symbolize the thirty years of war before independence. No primary legal text was opened, so it is hedged with 'said to'.

entries.remainingDoubts: The 1993 and 1995 flag proclamations themselves were not opened, so the color meanings rest on Wikipedia's 'government interpretation' and Britannica rather than the legal text. Population estimates for Eritrea vary widely between sources; the UN WPP 2024 figure is used as instructed.

funFact.value: Ethiopia keeps its own calendar with 13 months, twelve of 30 days plus a short one, and its year count runs seven to eight years behind the Western one.
funFact.note: Twelve 30-day months plus a 13th month of five or six days; the year number is eight years behind the Gregorian year until September and seven behind afterwards. 152 characters.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; worldstandards.eu lists Ethiopia as driving on the right. No disagreement found.

flag.text: Ethiopia's green, yellow and red date from 1897, when Emperor Menelik II flew them after defeating Italy at Adwa; many African nations later copied them as the Pan-African colors. Green is often read as development, yellow as hope and red as blood shed defending Ethiopia. The constitution says the star with equal rays, added in 1996, shows the hope of its peoples to live together in equality and unity; its blue circle is said to mean peace.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands green, yellow, red
reasons.why: First flown as a national flag on 11 October 1897 by Emperor Menelik II, a year after the victory over Italy at Adwa (1 March 1896); the 1897 flag had the order red, yellow, green, and the order was later reversed (after 1914) to the present green, yellow, red for reasons Wikipedia says are unknown. The colors had earlier religious and traditional use in Ethiopia. The constitution (Article 3) fixes green at top, yellow in the middle and red at the bottom in equal size.

reasons.feature: Green, yellow and red as the Pan-African colors
reasons.why: Wikipedia: several newly established African countries adopted these three colors in homage to Ethiopia's resistance against foreign occupation, so they are often called the Pan-African colors.
Represents development under Flag Proclamation No. 654/2009, as reported in the Wikipedia article's flag design symbolism section.
Represents hope under Proclamation No. 654/2009, as reported by Wikipedia.
Represents the blood shed in defense of Ethiopia under Proclamation No. 654/2009, as reported by Wikipedia.

The emblem was added in 1996 under the federal constitution (Wikipedia infobox gives 31 October 1996 for the current version) and enlarged by the 2009 law; the blue circular background stands for peace.

Article 3 of the constitution says the emblem reflects the hope of the Nations, Nationalities, Peoples and religious communities of Ethiopia to live together in equality and unity; Wikipedia adds that the star testifies to Ethiopia's bright future and the equal yellow rays are said to represent the equality of all Ethiopians.

entries.remainingDoubts: Proclamation No. 654/2009 was read only as summarized by Wikipedia, not in the gazette text; Wikipedia's infobox dates the 2009 modification 16 May 2009 while other sources give 28 August 2009, so no day is used in the text. The 2020 five-working-languages decision is reported by news media and Wikipedia; its official publication was not opened.

funFact.value: Madagascar broke away from India about 90 million years ago, and around 90 percent of its wildlife, including lemurs, lives nowhere else on Earth.
funFact.note: Wikipedia: split from the Indian subcontinent roughly 90 million years ago; over 90 percent of wildlife endemic; lemurs found naturally nowhere else. 146 characters.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; worldstandards.eu and the Wikipedia infobox both say right-hand traffic.

flag.text: Madagascar adopted its flag in 1958, when it gained self-rule from France, two years before independence. Red and white were the colors of the Merina kingdom, which ruled much of the island in the 1800s, linking the new nation to its past. Green is often said to stand for the coastal peoples and for hope. At the 1958 ceremony white was called purity and red sovereignty, but the constitution only describes the bands, with no official meaning.

reasons.feature: Vertical white band at the pole with red over green horizontal bands
reasons.why: Officially adopted 21 October 1958, one week after the Malagasy Republic was proclaimed on 14 October 1958 as an autonomous republic within the French Community, and before full independence on 26 June 1960; the 2010 constitution (Article 4) fixes this layout of three equal bands.

Red and white were the royal colors of the Merina kingdom, which ruled much of Madagascar from the late 1600s into the 1800s; the independence movement after World War II also used a white and red flag. Wikipedia notes early critics objected to the flag precisely because it used the Merina royal colors.

Not part of the royal colors; at the 1958 adoption ceremony it was called hope, Britannica says it is read as representing the coastal regions and peoples (the Hova commoner class in some readings), and the presidency's website also calls it hope and lush vegetation. No law gives this meaning.

Declared by Barinia Tsara of the Constituent National Assembly at the 1958 adoption ceremony (white is purity, red is sovereignty, green is hope), and repeated by Britannica with 'said to'; the president's office website offers a different reading (red national unity, green hope, white freedom). The 2010 constitution describes the design only and gives the colors no official meaning.

entries.remainingDoubts: Color meanings are not fixed in law; the two popular readings (1958 ceremony vs. the presidency's website) differ, so the entry hedges them. Wikipedia's country infobox and the area list disagree on total area (592,796 vs 587,041 km2); the list value is used as instructed.

funFact.note: Wikipedia lead: home to more species of fish than any other lake in the world, at least 700 cichlid species, almost all endemic. UNESCO page returned HTTP 403 so could not be opened as a second source. 129 characters.
