flag.text: Malawi's flag dates from independence on 6 July 1964. Its flag law says black stands for the people of Africa, red for the blood shed for African freedom, green for the evergreen land, and the red rising sun for the dawn of hope and freedom for the continent. Black, red and green are also the shared Pan-African colors. In 2010 a full white sun replaced it, but many objected and parliament restored the 1964 flag in 2012.

reasons.why: Represents the people of the continent of Africa, per the Protected Flag, Emblems and Names Act schedule as quoted by FOTW; Wikipedia gives the same reading (the indigenous people of the continent).
Represents the blood of the martyrs of African freedom (Wikipedia: the blood of their struggle).
Represents the evergreen nature of Malawi.

reasons.feature: Red rising sun with rays on the black band
reasons.why: Officially represents the dawn of hope and freedom for the whole continent of Africa; added in 1964 to set the national flag apart from the three plain bands of the Malawi Congress Party flag (the party-flag link comes from Britannica and FOTW, not Wikipedia).
Resembles the Pan-African flag designed by the Universal Negro Improvement Association (Garvey), with the red and black bands in reversed order.

Adopted 6 July 1964 at independence; replaced on 29 July 2010 by a red-black-green flag with a full centered white sun of 45 rays said to show the country's progress since independence; after public opposition parliament voted on 28 May 2012 to revert to the independence flag (Protected Flags, Emblems and Names Amendment Act).

entries.remainingDoubts: Chichewa's inclusion rests on its customary national-language status, not on a statute; English is the only language with legal official status. The flag's designer is not identified by any source opened. The official color meanings were read from FOTW's quotation of the Act schedule, not from the gazette itself; the reviewer re-checked only the Wikipedia flag article, which gives matching meanings and the 1964, 2010 and 2012 dates. The Malawi Congress Party link for the sun comes from the draft's Britannica/FOTW sources and was not re-verified. Population was not re-checked against the UN source directly.

flag.text: Mauritius adopted its flag at independence in 1968; retired schoolteacher Gurudutt Moher designed it. A 2022 national symbols law gives the official meanings: red for the struggle for freedom and independence, blue for the Indian Ocean around the island, yellow for the light of freedom shining over it, and green for farmland that stays green all year. The colors are also often said to match the four main political parties of the time.

reasons.why: The struggle for freedom and independence, per the National Flag, Arms of Mauritius, National Anthem and Other National Symbols of Mauritius Act 2022.
The Indian Ocean, in which Mauritius is situated.
The light of freedom shining over the island.
The agriculture of Mauritius and its green color throughout the twelve months of the year.

Often said to also stand for the four main political parties at independence (red Labour Party, blue PMSD, yellow IFB, green CAM), a reading presented in secondary sources, not in the Act, and credited with helping unite the country after the 1965 and 1968 riots.
Adopted 12 March 1968 at independence; designed by retired schoolteacher Gurudutt Moher, whose contribution was recognized posthumously in March 2018.

flag.text: Adopted in 1983, the flag grew out of that of FRELIMO, which won independence from Portugal in 1975. The constitution gives the meanings: green for the land, black for Africa, yellow for mineral wealth, white lines for peace, the red triangle for the fight against colonial rule, the star for solidarity with other peoples, the book for education, the hoe for farming and the AK-47 rifle for defense. In 2005 parliament voted to keep the rifle.

reasons.why: The riches of the soil, per the Constitution of Mozambique (Title XVI, Article 297, national symbols).
The African continent.
The riches of the subsoil (minerals).

reasons.feature: Thin white lines between the bands
reasons.why: Peace and the justice of the struggle of the Mozambican people.
Resistance to colonialism and the defense of national sovereignty.
The spirit of international solidarity of the Mozambican people; the opposition RENAMO has read it as a communist symbol, which supporters reject.
Education.
Production and the peasantry (farming).

Defense and vigilance; the constitution says only a gun, generally understood as the AK-47 used in the independence war. It is the only national flag with a modern firearm; RENAMO has asked for its removal as a symbol of violence, and after a 2005 redesign competition with 169 entries parliament voted 155 to 79 to keep the flag.

Derived from FRELIMO's first liberation-movement flag (green-black-yellow with white lines and a red triangle, without the star and weapons); the 1975 independence flag was replaced by the current layout on 1 May 1983. The green, black, yellow and red are also Pan-African colors.

flag.text: Rwanda adopted this flag on 31 December 2001, replacing a red, yellow and green flag with a black R that many people linked to the 1994 genocide. Artist and engineer Alphonse Kirimobenecyo designed it. The government says blue stands for happiness and peace, yellow for economic development and green for the hope of prosperity. The golden sun with 24 rays in the upper right stands for unity, openness and enlightenment.

reasons.feature: Blue band filling the top half
reasons.why: Officially stands for happiness and peace.
Officially stands for economic development.
Officially stands for hope of prosperity.

reasons.feature: Golden sun with 24 rays in the upper right corner
reasons.why: Officially stands for national unity and transparency and the enlightenment of the Rwandan people (Wikipedia, citing Rwandan sources; 'openness' in the text renders 'transparency'). Constitution Article 9 describes the sun with golden-yellow rays separated from it by a blue ring but gives no meaning.

reasons.feature: Adoption on 31 December 2001 replacing the 1961 red-yellow-green flag with a black R
reasons.why: The previous flag (adopted 28 January 1961, with the black R added in September 1961) had become associated with the 1994 genocide; the government announced in 1999 that the national symbols would change as part of reconciliation, and the new flag, coat of arms and anthem followed. Adoption date 31 December 2001 confirmed in the Wikipedia infobox.
Wikipedia names the Rwandan artist and engineer Alphonse Kirimobenecyo as designer; Britannica does not name a designer.

flag.text: Adopted in 1996 after multiparty politics returned, this flag mixes the colors of the two main parties: blue and yellow from the Democratic Party, red, white and green from the ruling party. Officially the five bands spreading from the lower left corner show a young country moving into the future. Blue is the sky and sea, yellow the sun, red the people working in unity and love, white social justice and harmony, green the land and nature.

reasons.feature: Five bands radiating from the lower left corner
reasons.why: Officially described as symbolizing a dynamic new country moving into the future (Wikipedia quotes 'The bands symbolise a dynamic new country moving into the future'; FOTW quotes the official description; Britannica gives no meaning for the arrangement).
Officially the sky and the sea that surround the Seychelles.
Officially the sun which gives light and life.

Officially the people and their determination to work for the future in unity and love (Wikipedia gives the shorter 'determination to work for the future'; 'in unity and love' is from the Britannica/FOTW wording).
Officially social justice and harmony.
Officially the land and natural environment.

Blue and yellow were the colors of the Seychelles Democratic Party (in government 1970-1977); red, white and green came from the Seychelles People's United Party / Seychelles People's Progressive Front (today United Seychelles), which ruled from the 1977 coup and whose colors made up the 1977-1996 flag. After multiparty democracy returned in 1993 the flag was redesigned to be non-partisan.

Established by the National Symbols Act (Act 3 of 1996); the bill was published on 8 January 1996 (Wikipedia's infobox adoption date, confirmed) and the flag took effect on 18 June 1996, National Day (Britannica's date).

entries.remainingDoubts: Adoption date differs by source (8 January 1996 on Wikipedia, 18 June 1996 on Britannica); FOTW reconciles them as publication vs. effective date, so the text says only 1996. Wikipedia's infobox names Philip Uzice as designer, but neither Britannica nor FOTW confirms it, so no designer is named in the text. flag.text: Mohammed Awale Liban designed this flag, first raised on 12 October 1954 when southern Somalia was a United Nations trust territory. The light blue honors the United Nations, which helped the country toward independence. The white star is called the Star of Unity; its five points were meant to stand for the five areas of the Horn of Africa where Somalis have long lived, two of which joined in 1960 to form independent Somalia.

reasons.why: Chosen as a tribute to the United Nations, under whose trusteeship (Italian administration, 1950-1960) the territory moved to independence; the designer is quoted saying the blue stands for the United Nations who helped reach the dream of independence.

reasons.feature: White five-pointed star in the center (Star of Unity)
reasons.why: The designer intended each point to stand for one of five areas of the Horn of Africa inhabited by Somalis and divided by colonial borders (former British Somaliland, former Italian Somaliland, Djibouti, the Somali region of Ethiopia and northeastern Kenya); only the first two united as Somalia in 1960. Reported here as documented intent, without endorsement.

First officially hoisted on 12 October 1954 after approval by the trust territory's legislative council; became the national flag at independence and union on 1 July 1960. The 2012 Provisional Constitution Article 6 describes it as a light blue rectangle with a white star of five equal points in the center, without giving a meaning.
Named as designer by Wikipedia and FOTW (the latter with his own account of drafting it overnight for the council); Britannica does not name a designer.

entries.remainingDoubts: The constitution does not formally fix Mogadishu as capital (Article 9 defers it), though it is the capital in practice and per ownerRules. Arabic is constitutionally the 'second language' rather than co-equal. Landmarks were not confirmed from an opened page, and Laas Geel lies in the self-declared Somaliland region. The exact coastline length was not confirmed in the opened page beyond 'longest on mainland Africa'. The star's five-point symbolism is politically sensitive and is reported neutrally as the designer's documented intent. Within the verification time budget the Somalia flag facts were not re-fetched; they rest on the draft's Wikipedia, Britannica and FOTW sources.

entries.name: South Sudan

officialName.note: Article 1 of the 2011 Transitional Constitution: the state 'shall be known as The Republic of South Sudan'.

capital.note: Article 50 of the Transitional Constitution names the City of Juba as the National Capital and seat of government. Older plans to build a new capital at Ramciel have not changed the law in force. Matches the seed rule.

population.note: UN World Population Prospects 2024 revision, mid-2024 estimate 11,943,408, rounded to 3 significant figures. The UN data portal API refused the request (HTTP 401), so the WPP 2024 figure was read from Worldometers' copy of the UN table; its 2023 value (11,483,374) matches the Wikipedia UN list exactly. Rounding re-checked: 11.94 million -> 11,900,000.

areaSqKm.note: Total area (land plus inland water) as given in Wikipedia's list, rank 41; the list gives no land/water split for South Sudan and attaches a footnote (likely about the disputed border zone) that was not read.

languages.note: Article 6(2): English is the official working language and language of instruction. Article 6(1) makes all indigenous languages national languages, but none is named, so only English is listed, as the seed rule requires.

currency.note: ISO 4217 code SSP; introduced 18 July 2011. The Wikipedia infobox shows no dedicated symbol, so the ISO code is used.

landmarks.note: All three are named in the Wikipedia country article; the Sudd is one of the world's largest wetlands, Boma hosts the great antelope migration, Nimule lies on the Ugandan border by the Nile.

funFact.value: Millions of antelope move each year across South Sudan's plains to Ethiopia and back, one of the largest land animal migrations on Earth.
funFact.note: 137 characters. Wikipedia's country article describes the Boma migration of over a million antelope; a 2024 African Parks aerial survey (reported by The EastAfrican and Afrik21, seen via search summaries) counted about six million animals in the Boma-Badingilo-Jonglei landscape. 'One of the largest' is used rather than 'the largest' to stay durable.

driveSide.note: Both sources say South Sudan drives on the right, despite bordering left-driving Uganda and Kenya. Agrees with the seed (leftHand false).

flag.text: South Sudan's flag began as the banner of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement, which fought for the south's freedom from Sudan. It became the region's flag in 2005 after a peace deal and the national flag at independence in 2011. The government says black stands for the people, red for blood shed for independence, white for peace, green for the land and its wealth, the blue triangle for the Nile and the yellow star for unity and hope.

reasons.feature: Overall design: black, red and green bands with thin white edges, blue triangle at the flagpole with a yellow star
reasons.why: A version of the design was the flag of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement/Army during the civil war against the north. It was adopted as the flag of Southern Sudan on 9 July 2005 after the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and became the national flag at independence on 9 July 2011. No individual designer is identified in Wikipedia or Britannica.
The South Sudanese government specifies that black represents the people of South Sudan.
Officially the blood that was shed for the independence of the country.
Officially the country's agricultural and natural wealth, the land, and progress.

reasons.feature: Thin white stripes between the bands
reasons.why: Officially peace, won after many years of war.

reasons.feature: Blue triangle at the flagpole side
reasons.why: Officially the waters of the Nile River, a source of life for the country.
Officially unity (of the states of South Sudan), hope and determination for all the people. Wikipedia's flag article does not link the star to the Star of Bethlehem, so that reading is left out.

reasons.feature: Light sky-blue shade of the triangle and upright star
reasons.why: On 25 August 2023 the Media Authority of South Sudan issued an advisory identifying the correct flag as having a light blue triangle and an upright star; dark-blue or tilted-star versions may no longer be distributed.

entries.remainingDoubts: The official color meanings were read from Wikipedia's summary of government statements (re-checked in this pass: Wikipedia explicitly attributes them to the South Sudanese government), Britannica, and search snippets of Eye Radio/FOTW rather than a primary gov.ss page (none could be opened). No designer is named for the flag in any source. The population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 because the UN API returned 401. The area list footnote on South Sudan's row was not read. The currency has no symbol in Wikipedia's infobox, so the ISO code is used. The migration fun fact relies on news reports of a 2024 survey seen via search summaries plus Wikipedia's older 'second-largest' description.

entries.name: Uganda

officialName.note: The 1995 Constitution (rev. 2017) uses 'Republic of Uganda'; Wikipedia infobox agrees.

capital.note: Article 5 of the Constitution: Kampala, located in Buganda, shall be the capital city for Uganda. Matches the seed rule.

population.note: UN World Population Prospects 2024 revision, mid-2024 estimate 50,015,092, rounded to 3 significant figures (third digit is 0, so 50,000,000; the '4 figures if the third digit would be 5' rule does not apply). Read from Worldometers' copy of the UN table because the UN data portal API returned 401; its 2023 value (48,656,601) matches the Wikipedia UN list exactly. Note the 2024 national census counted about 45.9 million, lower than the UN estimate.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia's list (rank 79): land 200,520 km2 plus inland water 41,030 km2 (17.0% water, mostly Lake Victoria and other lakes). The Wikipedia country infobox gives a slightly different 241,038 km2; the list figure is used per the field rule.

languages.note: Article 6(1): the official language of Uganda is English; Article 6(2): Swahili shall be the second official language, to be used as Parliament prescribes. Matches the seed rule.

currency.note: ISO 4217 code UGX; symbol USh (also written /=). Current shilling introduced 1987.

landmarks.note: All three are named as main attractions in Wikipedia's Tourism in Uganda article; Bwindi is home to about half of the world's mountain gorillas.

funFact.value: The White Nile begins its long journey to the Mediterranean at Jinja in Uganda, flowing out of Lake Victoria, the world's second-largest freshwater lake.
funFact.note: 153 characters. Jinja article: the town sits on the north shore of Lake Victoria at the source of the White Nile. Uganda article: Lake Victoria is the world's second-largest freshwater lake by surface area.

driveSide.note: Both sources say Uganda drives on the left, a legacy of the British Protectorate. Agrees with the seed (leftHand true).

flag.text: Uganda's flag was adopted at independence on 9 October 1962. Justice minister Grace Ibingira is credited with the design, whose colors came from the winning Uganda People's Congress party. Black is said to stand for the people, yellow for sunshine and red for brotherhood. The crowned crane in the white circle is the national bird; British officials had chosen it as Uganda's badge because it belonged to no single region.

reasons.feature: Six horizontal bands of black, yellow and red, repeated twice
reasons.why: The colors were those of the Uganda People's Congress, whose first party flag was the basis of the design after it won the April 1962 election; it replaced a provisional March 1962 flag of green, blue and green vertical bands in the colors of the then-ruling Democratic Party. Adopted 9 October 1962, the day of independence; Grace Ibingira, then Minister of Justice, is credited with the design, though other artists have claimed it. The National Flag and Armorial Ensigns Act of 1962 governs its use.

Widely stated (Whitney Smith in Britannica, repeated by Wikipedia) to stand for the Ugandan people; no primary government or legal text giving the meaning could be opened, so the reading is hedged as 'is said to'.
Widely stated to stand for sunshine (Africa's sunshine); same sourcing as the black bands.
Widely stated to stand for brotherhood, red being the color of the blood that connects all Africans; same sourcing as the black bands.

reasons.feature: Grey crowned crane with red and gold crest in a white circle at the center
reasons.why: The crane is Uganda's national bird. The British chose it for the colonial badge because they did not want to use any existing symbol tied to a specific region or kingdom, and it was kept as the chief national symbol at independence. It is also traditionally said to represent good fortune, long life and wealth among the Baganda.

entries.remainingDoubts: The Uganda Ministry of Foreign Affairs 'National Symbols' pages returned 404, so the color meanings rest on Whitney Smith (Britannica) and Wikipedia; Wikipedia attributes them to Smith rather than to a law, so the color reasons are labeled traditional and the text hedges with 'is said to'. Wikipedia notes other artists (e.g. Semei Nyai Matia in 2007) have claimed the design besides Ibingira. The crane's raised-leg meaning (nation moving forward) is widely repeated but not in the sources opened, so it is left out. Population is from Worldometers' copy of WPP 2024 (UN API returned 401).

entries.name: Zambia

officialName.note: The Constitution (1991, rev. 2016) refers throughout to the Republic of Zambia; Wikipedia infobox agrees.

capital.note: Lusaka per Wikipedia and the seed rule; the constitutional article naming the capital was not reached because the constitution fetch was truncated.

population.note: UN World Population Prospects 2024 revision, mid-2024 estimate 21,314,956, rounded to 3 significant figures. Read from Worldometers' copy of the UN table because the UN data portal API returned 401; its 2023 value (20,723,965) matches the Wikipedia UN list exactly.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia's list (rank 38): land 743,390 km2 plus inland water 9,220 km2 (1.2% water). The Wikipedia country infobox gives 752,617 km2; the list figure is used per the field rule.

languages.note: Article 258(1) of the Constitution as amended in 2016: the official language of Zambia is English; 258(2) allows other languages for instruction and administration. The constituteproject page was truncated before Article 258, so the wording was confirmed via a search snippet quoting it. Seven recognized regional languages (Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga, Lozi, Lunda, Luvale, Kaonde) are not official and are left out. Matches the seed rule.

currency.note: ISO 4217 code ZMW since the 2013 redenomination (formerly ZMK); symbols K and ZK; subdivided into 100 ngwee.

landmarks.note: All three are named in the Wikipedia country article. Victoria Falls and Lake Kariba lie on the Zambezi border with Zimbabwe and are shared; the Zambian side of the falls is in Mosi-oa-Tunya National Park near Livingstone.

funFact.value: Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River is known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders, for the spray that rises high above the gorge.
funFact.note: 142 characters. Wikipedia's Zambia article: David Livingstone named the falls in 1855; locally they are known as Mosi-o-Tunya, 'thundering smoke'.

driveSide.note: Both sources say Zambia drives on the left, a legacy of British rule as Northern Rhodesia. Agrees with the seed (leftHand true).

flag.text: Zambia's flag was adopted at independence on 24 October 1964 and designed by Gabriel Ellison, based on the flag of the party that led the country to freedom. The stripes sit in the lower right corner, with the eagle flying above them. Green is said to mean farming and plants, red the freedom struggle, black the people and orange copper and mineral wealth. The fish eagle is said to mean freedom and rising above the nation's problems.

reasons.feature: Overall design: green background with the eagle and three stripes placed in the lower right corner, away from the flagpole
reasons.why: Designed by Gabriel Ellison and adopted on 24 October 1964, the day Northern Rhodesia became independent Zambia, replacing the British colonial flag. Britannica traces it to the flag of the United National Independence Party, whose green background was kept with the other colors moved to stripes at the outer end (Wikipedia's flag article does not mention the party link). The design was specified in the National Flag and Armorial Ensigns Act of 1965. In 1996 the green was made brighter and lighter and the eagle redrawn to match the coat of arms.

Widely stated to stand for the nation's agriculture and lush plant life. Wikipedia attributes the color meanings to Whitney Smith (Britannica) and says the 1965 Act gives only design specifications, so the reading is hedged with 'is said to'.
Widely stated to stand for the nation's struggle for freedom; same sourcing as the green background.
Widely stated to stand for the Zambian people and all black Africans; same sourcing as the green background.

reasons.feature: Orange stripe and orange color of the eagle
reasons.why: Widely stated to stand for the land's copper, mineral wealth and natural resources; copper mining has been central to Zambia's economy since deposits were found along the Kafue River in 1895. Same sourcing as the green background.

reasons.feature: African fish eagle in flight above the stripes
reasons.why: Widely stated to represent freedom and the people's ability to rise above the nation's problems; the same eagle appears on the coat of arms. Same sourcing as the green background.

entries.remainingDoubts: Wikipedia's flag article cites Whitney Smith (Britannica) for the color and eagle meanings and states that the 1965 National Flag and Armorial Ensigns Act only describes the design, so the meanings are labeled traditional and the text hedges with 'is said to'; Zambian government pages that repeat these meanings were not opened. The UNIP party-flag origin comes from Britannica only; Wikipedia's flag article does not mention it. The constitutional article naming Lusaka as capital was not reached (page truncated); Article 258 on English was confirmed via a search snippet. Population is from Worldometers' copy of WPP 2024 (UN API returned 401). Victoria Falls and Lake Kariba are shared with Zimbabwe.

entries.name: Zimbabwe

capital.note: Seed ownerRule and Wikipedia infobox agree: Harare is the capital and largest city.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, medium variant, mid-2024 estimate 16,634,373 (read via Worldometers, which attributes it to WPP 2024); rounded to 3 significant figures. The UN download page returned 404 in both the drafting and the review session, so the figure was not read directly from population.un.org.

areaSqKm.note: Total area including inland water: 386,850 km2 land plus about 3,910 km2 water (about 1%), per Wikipedia's list; the Zimbabwe infobox gives the same 390,757 km2.

languages.note: Verified against the constitutional text (Constitute Project): Section 6(1) of the 2013 Constitution lists exactly 16 officially recognised languages in this order: Chewa, Chibarwe, English, Kalanga, Koisan, Nambya, Ndau, Ndebele, Shangani, Shona, sign language, Sotho, Tonga, Tswana, Venda and Xhosa. The entry uses the English forms 'Khoisan' and 'Zimbabwean Sign Language' from the Wikipedia infobox, matching the South Africa entry's style, and lists sign language last.

currency.note: Zimbabwe Gold (ISO code ZWG, symbol ZiG) has been the official currency since 8 April 2024. Zimbabwe runs a multicurrency system: the US dollar (and some other foreign currencies) remain legal tender nationwide, authorised through 31 December 2030, and the US dollar is the one most used. Two currencies are listed because both are legal tender nationwide; if the app wants strictly one, use 'Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG)'. Not re-fetched in the review session.

landmarks.note: Great Zimbabwe is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986). Victoria Falls on the Zambezi is shared with Zambia but lies on Zimbabwe's border and is its best-known sight; Hwange is the country's largest national park. The latter two are well established but were not separately fetched. Hand edit after the workflow: Victoria Falls is listed under Zambia, so Matobo Hills (UNESCO World Heritage) takes its place here.

funFact.value: The country is named after Great Zimbabwe, a stone city begun in the 11th century; the name comes from Shona words meaning large houses of stone.
funFact.note: 145 characters. Wikipedia: built from the 11th century, occupied to the 15th; name from Shona 'dzimba-dza-mabwe' (large houses of stone), with an alternative reading 'venerated houses'; the country took the name at independence in 1980.

driveSide.note: Seed says left. The Wikipedia traffic article's Africa section says Rhodesia (present-day Zambia and Zimbabwe) was given left-hand traffic under British rule; no source disagrees.

flag.text: Adopted at independence in 1980, the stripes copy the ZANU-PF party flag in the Pan-African green, gold, red and black of many African flags. Officially green is for farmland, gold for minerals, red for blood shed in the liberation war and black for the black majority. The white triangle means peace and the red star the nation's aspirations. The gold bird copies soapstone carvings found at Great Zimbabwe. The black edge has no stated meaning.

reasons.feature: Seven horizontal stripes in green, gold, red, black, red, gold, green
reasons.why: The colours and their order are based on the flag of the ruling party ZANU-PF, and they are the Pan-African colours used by many African flags (Wikipedia: the design 'incorporated the pan-African colours of yellow, black, green and red'). The official government page confirms the flag was accepted on 22 March 1980 and first raised at midnight on 17/18 April 1980 to mark independence; Flags of the World says it was established by Presidential Order No. 16 of 1980, later the Flag of Zimbabwe Act (Act 22/1985).
Official Government of Zimbabwe page (verified): green 'represents vegetation and agriculture'.
Official Government of Zimbabwe page (verified): yellow 'represents the country's mineral wealth' (Wikipedia adds: predominantly gold).
Official Government of Zimbabwe page (verified): red 'represents the blood shed during the war of the liberation' (Wikipedia: the first and second Chimurenga).
Official Government of Zimbabwe page (verified): black 'represents the black majority'.

reasons.feature: White triangle at the flagpole side
reasons.why: Official Government of Zimbabwe page (verified): the white triangle 'represents peace'.

Official Government of Zimbabwe page (verified): the red star 'represents the nation's aspirations'. Wikipedia adds that this is often taken to mean socialism as promoted by the ruling party; that reading is not the government's wording, so the text uses only the official meaning.

reasons.feature: Gold Zimbabwe Bird on the star
reasons.why: The national emblem, copied from soapstone bird carvings found at the ruins of Great Zimbabwe; Wikipedia (verified) says the initial 1980 design did not include the bird, which was added at the suggestion of Cedric Herbert, who pointed out its uniqueness and history. The government page says it 'represents the National Emblem'.

reasons.feature: Thin black edge of the white triangle
reasons.why: Visible in the flag image as a thin black line along the two long sides of the triangle, merging with the central black stripe. The government page gives no border symbolism (verified) and the Wikipedia article gives none either.

entries.remainingDoubts: 1) Currency: two currencies are listed because the US dollar is legal tender nationwide alongside Zimbabwe Gold under the multicurrency system (authorised through 2030); the owner may prefer 'Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG)' alone, and the arrangement could change; this was not re-fetched in review. 2) Population was taken from Worldometers' reproduction of UN WPP 2024 (16,634,373), not from the UN site directly, which returned 404 again in review. 3) Language spelling: the constitution (verified at Constitute Project) writes 'Koisan' and 'sign language'; the entry uses 'Khoisan' and 'Zimbabwean Sign Language' per the Wikipedia infobox and moves sign language to the end. 4) Drive side 'Left' rests on the seed and the Wikipedia traffic article's history section. 5) The Flag of Zimbabwe Act (Act 22/1985) and Presidential Order No. 16 of 1980 are cited only via Flags of the World; the color meanings were verified on the government web page, not in the Act's text. 6) Victoria Falls and Hwange National Park were not individually verified by a fetched page. 7) Flag text revised in review to name the Pan-African origin explicitly; it is 446 characters, within the 450 limit.

entries.name: Botswana

capital.note: Per seed ownerRules and Wikipedia infobox.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 medium variant 2,521,139 as reproduced by Worldometers (the UN data portal API returned 401); Wikipedia's UN list only showed 1 July 2023 = 2,480,244, consistent with it. Rounded to 3 s.f. (third digit 2, so 3 s.f. applies).

areaSqKm.note: Total area from Wikipedia's area list: 566,730 land + 15,000 water (CIA-sourced row). The Botswana article's infobox gives 581,730.

languages.note: English is official, Setswana (Tswana) is the national language; both listed per seed ownerRules.

currency.note: Infobox: Pula (BWP). The common symbol is P; ISO code used because no opened page confirmed the symbol.

landmarks.note: Okavango Delta (UNESCO) and Chobe named in Tourism in Botswana; Tsodilo Hills confirmed in Botswana, UNESCO-listed 2001, over 4,500 rock paintings.

funFact.value: Botswana's motto and its money share one name: pula, the Setswana word for rain, which is precious in a country that is mostly Kalahari Desert.
funFact.note: 143 characters. Motto Pula (rain), currency pula, about 70% of territory in the Kalahari per Wikipedia.

driveSide.note: Wikipedia infobox: drives on the left; matches seed leftHand=true.

flag.text: Botswana adopted this flag on 30 September 1966, the day it became independent from Britain; George Winstanley designed it. Light blue stands for water, above all rain, scarce in a mostly desert country whose motto Pula means rain. The black band with white edges officially stands for harmony between black and white people, a contrast to apartheid South Africa, and the colors also match the zebra, the national animal.

reasons.feature: Light blue upper and lower bands
reasons.why: Stand for water and rainfall, scarce and precious in an arid country; linked to the national motto Pula (rain). Verified: Wikipedia says the blue background represents water and rainfall, a resource crucial to the agriculture of the arid nation.

reasons.feature: Black central band with thin white edges
reasons.why: Represents racial harmony and the plural racial make-up of the nation (government and embassy wording; Wikipedia: the black central stripe bordered by two white stripes represents racial harmony).

First hoisted at midnight on 30 September 1966, independence day. George Winstanley ran a design competition, judged all entries hopeless and designed the flag himself. Proportions (2:3, stripe widths in 24ths) are fixed in the Botswana Emblems Law.
Wikipedia: the flag's adoption was a symbolic rejection of the system of apartheid, its themes of racial equality contrasting with policies of racial hierarchy in neighbouring South Africa.

reasons.feature: Black and white matching the zebra
reasons.why: The embassy's national symbols page says the zebra was chosen as national animal partly because its black and white matches the flag's colors of racial harmony. Wikipedia's flag article does not mention the zebra, so this rests on the embassy page alone.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population is WPP 2024 mid-2024 via Worldometers' reproduction, not the UN portal itself (API returned 401). Area: list gives 582,000 while the country article gives 581,730; I used the list per the rules. Currency symbol P not confirmed from an opened page, so ISO code used. The zebra link comes only from the embassy page (botswanamission.ch), which I did not re-open in this verification pass; Wikipedia's flag article confirms the designer, date, water/rain and racial-harmony meanings and the apartheid contrast but is silent on the zebra. The gov.bw site was not opened.

entries.name: Eswatini

capital.note: Exact wording from seed ownerRules; Wikipedia: Mbabane executive, Lobamba legislative (and royal) capital.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 medium variant 1,242,822 as reproduced by Worldometers; Wikipedia's UN list showed 1 July 2023 = 1,230,506. Rounded to 3 s.f.

areaSqKm.note: Total from Wikipedia's area list (17,200 land + 160 water, rounded). The Eswatini article says 17,364.

languages.note: critic: The existing South Africa entry in app/src/main/java/com/example/data/model/AfricaCatalog.kt names the same language 'Swati'; the same language should carry one name across the catalog (the entry's own note already flags this).

currency.note: ISO SZL; symbols L/E are ambiguous so the ISO code is used. The South African rand is widely accepted and pegged 1:1 via the Common Monetary Area, but Wikipedia says it ceased to be legal tender in 1986, so only one currency is listed.

landmarks.note: Hlane is the country's largest protected area; Mlilwane is named in Tourism in Eswatini; Sibebe is a granite mountain 10 km from Mbabane, often called the world's second-largest monolith.

funFact.value: In 2018 King Mswati III renamed Swaziland as Eswatini, which means land of the Swazis, partly to avoid confusion with Switzerland.
funFact.note: 130 characters; Wikipedia gives the meaning and the Switzerland confusion as part of the reason. The 2018 date is a historical event, not a dated statistic.

driveSide.note: The LHT article names Eswatini among territories where Britain introduced left-hand traffic; matches seed leftHand=true. The Eswatini infobox driving side was not captured by the fetch.

flag.text: The flag comes from a banner King Sobhuza II gave in 1941 to Swazi soldiers sent to the Second World War, and became the national flag at independence in 1968. Officially red stands for past battles, blue for peace and stability and yellow for natural resources. The black and white ox-hide shield shows black and white people living in peace, two spears mean protection, and the stick carries feather tassels that only the king may use.

reasons.why: Based on the military flag King Sobhuza II gave in 1941 to the Swazi Pioneer Corps; first hoisted 25 April 1967, the day the king took the pledge of oath; officially adopted 6 October 1968 at independence (crwflags cites Act No. 36).
Stands for past battles (Wikipedia: the red stands for past battles).
Stand for peace and stability.
Stand for the resources of Eswatini.

reasons.feature: Black and white Nguni ox-hide shield
reasons.why: Government wording: the shield's color shows that white and black people live in peaceful coexistence in Eswatini; the shield and two spears symbolise protection from the country's enemies.

reasons.feature: Two spears and staff with feather tassels (injobo)
reasons.why: The tassels are bunches of feathers of the widowbird and the lourie, which are only used by the king. Wikipedia: in 2011 some versions of the flag began using black (dark grey in the image) for the tassels to match the widowbird's natural color.

entries.remainingDoubts: The gov.sz national flag page and Britannica's Eswatini flag page could not be opened (503/404); meanings rely on Wikipedia and crwflags quoting a government leaflet. Wikipedia's flag article confirmed the 1941 origin, 25 April 1967 first hoisting, 6 October 1968 adoption, the color meanings, the shield and spear meanings and the king-only tassels; the 2011 change is described there as some versions switching the tassels to black to match the widowbird, so the draft's 'stylized blue to grey' wording was corrected. 'Act No. 36' comes from crwflags and was not verified by me. Legal-tender status of the rand is contested between sources, so only the lilangeni is listed. Language spelling 'Swazi' vs the app's existing 'Swati' should be harmonized by the owner.

quizCapital.note: critic: Eswatini's capital string names two cities but the entry has no quizCapital; the rules require quizCapital = the first city in the string.

entries.name: Lesotho

capital.note: Per seed ownerRules and Wikipedia.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 medium variant 2,337,423 as reproduced by Worldometers; Wikipedia's UN list showed 1 July 2023 = 2,311,472. Rounded to 3 s.f. (The Lesotho article's own 2.1 million figure is a different, national estimate.)

areaSqKm.note: Total from Wikipedia's area list; all land, no inland water counted. Matches the country article.

languages.note: Per seed ownerRules and Wikipedia infobox; Xhosa and Phuthi are only recognized, not official.

currency.note: Two currencies listed because Wikipedia states both the loti and the rand are legal tender in Lesotho (Common Monetary Area, 1:1 peg). Loti symbol L/M is ambiguous so ISO code used; rand symbol R matches the existing South Africa entry.

landmarks.note: Maletsunyane Falls: 192 m single-drop waterfall near Semonkong. Thaba Bosiu (Moshoeshoe I's stronghold) and Katse Dam (Lesotho Highlands Water Project) are named in the Lesotho article.

funFact.value: Lesotho is the only country that lies entirely above 1,000 meters; even its lowest point is about 1,400 meters above sea level.
funFact.note: 127 characters; Wikipedia: only independent state entirely above 1,000 m, lowest point 1,400 m (highest low point of any country).

driveSide.note: The LHT article names Lesotho among territories where Britain introduced left-hand traffic; matches seed leftHand=true.

flag.text: Lesotho raised this flag on 4 October 2006, the 40th anniversary of its independence, replacing a 1987 design with a shield, spear and club from the time of military rule. Blue stands for rain, white for peace and green for prosperity, echoing the national motto Khotso, Pula, Nala. In the center is a mokorotlo, the straw hat of the Basotho people, white on the first flag of 1966 and black here to represent Lesotho as a black nation.

reasons.why: Adopted on the 40th anniversary of independence from Britain, to reflect a state at peace internally and with its only neighbour South Africa; the bill passed the National Assembly on 18 September 2006 with 84 in favour, 18 against and two abstaining, then the Senate.

The 1987 flag, introduced on 20 January 1987 after a military coup that ousted the Basotho National Party, showed a light brown Basotho shield with an assegai (spear) and knobkierrie (club); the 2006 redesign moved away from military imagery.
Blue represents the sky or rain, white peace and green prosperity, as stated for the 2006 flag.

reasons.feature: Link of the colors to the motto Khotso, Pula, Nala
reasons.why: Peace, rain and prosperity are the three words of the national motto on the coat of arms, so the colors are commonly said to echo it; Wikipedia's flag article itself does not state the link, hence the hedged 'echoing' in the text.

The traditional cone-shaped straw hat is a symbol of the Basotho people; the 1966 independence flag featured a prominent white mokorotlo, and the 2006 proposals showed a brown hat that was changed to black in order to represent Lesotho as a black nation.

entries.remainingDoubts: The text of the 2006 flag legislation and the National University of Lesotho paper on the flag could not be opened (503), so color meanings rest on Wikipedia and Britannica; Wikipedia's flag article confirmed the date, the 84-18-2 vote, the 1987 coup flag, the color meanings, the white 1966 hat and the brown-to-black change, but does not mention the motto, so the motto link is worded as 'echoing' and labelled traditional. entries.name: Namibia

flag.text: Adopted at independence in 1990, the flag uses the blue, red and green of SWAPO, which led the fight for independence, as a red diagonal band between blue and green triangles. The committee said red is for the people and their heroism, white for peace and unity, green for plants and farms, and blue for the sky, the Atlantic and rain. The gold sun means life and energy; its twelve rays are said to stand for twelve groups of Namibians.

reasons.feature: Diagonal blue, red and green layout
reasons.why: The three colors were those of the SWAPO flag (a horizontal blue, red and green flag of the liberation movement, flown at the UN 1976-1990); SWAPO's 1989 election win made its colors the basis of the national design, which the sub-committee turned into a diagonal arrangement. The SWAPO link rests on the Britannica article cited in the drafting pass; the Wikipedia flag article as summarized in the review pass did not restate it.

A national competition (870 entries per Wikipedia, about 835 per Britannica) was narrowed by the National Symbols Sub-Committee to three finalists by Theo Jankowski (Rehoboth), Don Stevenson (Windhoek) and Ortrud Clay (Luderitz), whose designs were combined; the Constituent Assembly adopted the flag on 2 February 1990 and it was first hoisted at independence on 21 March 1990. The constitution (Article 2, Schedule 6) makes it the national flag.

Judge Hans Berker, chairman of the National Symbols Sub-Committee, explained that red represents Namibia's most important resource, its people, their heroism and their determination to build a future of equal opportunity for all (re-checked on Wikipedia's Flag of Namibia article).

reasons.feature: White edges along the red band
reasons.why: In the sub-committee chairman's explanation white represents peace, unity, tranquility and harmony; Britannica (per the drafting pass) adds that State Herald Frederick Brownell recommended the white borders to separate the red from the blue and green. The Brownell detail was not re-verified in the review pass.
In the sub-committee chairman's explanation green symbolizes vegetation and agricultural resources (re-checked on Wikipedia).
In the sub-committee chairman's explanation blue represents the clear Namibian sky and the Atlantic Ocean, the country's precious water resources and rain (re-checked on Wikipedia).

reasons.feature: Golden sun in the upper left
reasons.why: In the sub-committee chairman's explanation the sun represents life and energy, and its golden-yellow color the wealth of the country (re-checked on Wikipedia).

The flag image confirms twelve triangular rays. Wikipedia's Flag of Namibia article, quoting the sub-committee chairman's official symbolism, says the twelve rays represent the twelve ethnicities of Namibia that make up most of the population, divided into four main groups of three. Britannica does not repeat this and the constitution gives no color meanings, so the text hedges with are said to.

criticApplied.value: Cameroon chose three upright bands of green, red and yellow in 1957, the second country after Ghana to adopt these Pan-African colors. Red is usually read as the color of unity, and the gold star in the center is called the star of unity. Yellow is said to stand for the sun and the northern grasslands, green for the southern forests. Two stars marked the union of the former French and British parts from 1961 until one star was adopted in 1975.
criticApplied.reason: The current text says Cameroon was 'the second country to use these Pan-African colors', which contradicts the Ghana text (first used by Ethiopia; Ghana's flag of March 1957 came before Cameroon's law of 26 October 1957). Wikipedia says Cameroon was the second state to adopt them, i.e. after Ghana. 447 characters.

criticApplied.value: Ethiopia's green, yellow and red date from 1897, when Emperor Menelik II flew them after defeating Italy at Adwa; many African nations later copied them as the Pan-African colors. Green is often read as development, yellow as hope and red as blood shed defending Ethiopia. The constitution says the star with equal rays, added in 1996, shows the hope of its peoples to live together in equality and unity; its blue circle is said to mean peace.
criticApplied.reason: The text states 'A 2009 flag law says green means development...'. The Wikipedia symbolism section giving those meanings cites no source and the article does not attribute them to Proclamation 654/2009 (it only says the proclamation mandated emblem usage); Britannica gives different meanings (green labour/development/fertility, yellow hope/justice/equality, red sacrifice) and cites no law. The color meanings are therefore hedged as a common reading, and only the emblem meaning, which is in the constitution (Article 3), is stated plainly. 444 characters.

criticApplied.value: Zambia's flag was adopted at independence on 24 October 1964 and designed by Gabriel Ellison, based on the flag of the party that led the country to freedom. The stripes sit in the lower right corner, with the eagle flying above them. Green is said to mean farming and plants, red the freedom struggle, black the people and orange copper and mineral wealth. The fish eagle is said to mean freedom and rising above the nation's problems.
criticApplied.reason: The current text says 'The stripes and eagle sit in the lower right corner', but the eagle flies above the stripe block in the upper part of the right half (standard description: an eagle in flight over a block of three vertical stripes in the lower right corner). No page was opened for this; it is the flag's standard description and visible in the image. 436 characters.
The Somalia text says 'The light blue honors the United Nations', and Djibouti and Botswana list the same shade as 'Light Blue'; 'Blue' is inconsistent with both the text and those entries.
The Senegal text calls the middle band 'gold' twice, and Mali, whose flag shares the same Mali Federation bands, lists 'Gold'; flagColors should match the entry's own text and the Mali entry.
The other three dual-legal-tender entries in this batch (ZW, LS, NA) join the two currencies with ', '; Liberia alone uses ' and '.
Benin's capital string names two cities but the entry has no quizCapital; the rules require quizCapital = the first (constitutional) city, as the existing South Africa entry and the CI/BI entries do.
Eswatini's capital string names two cities but the entry has no quizCapital; the rules require quizCapital = the first city in the string.

criticApplied.value: Adopted on 4 August 1984, when Thomas Sankara's revolutionary government renamed Upper Volta as Burkina Faso, the flag replaced a black, white and red one whose stripes stood for the three Volta rivers. Red and green with a yellow star are Pan-African colors drawn from Ethiopia's flag. Red is often said to stand for the revolution, green for farming and natural riches, and the yellow star for the light that guides it.
criticApplied.reason: Date style: 8 texts (BF, GN, GW, LR, AO, CF, TD, CG) write US-style 'August 4, 1984' while the other 14 dated texts in the batch write '4 August 1984'; harmonized to the majority day-month form. Content unchanged. 421 characters.

criticApplied.value: Guinea adopted this flag on 10 November 1958, weeks after leaving French rule. The upright bands follow the French flag's layout, but the colors are the Pan-African red, yellow and green, taken from Ghana's 1957 flag. President Sékou Touré said red stands for the blood of those who died fighting colonial rule and for work, yellow for gold and the sun, and green for the land's plants, matching the motto Work, Justice, Solidarity.
criticApplied.reason: Date style harmonized to day-month like the rest of the batch; content unchanged. 432 characters.

criticApplied.value: Adopted on 24 September 1973, when Guinea-Bissau declared independence from Portugal, the flag copies the 1961 flag of the PAIGC independence party, itself modeled on Ghana's flag and its Pan-African colors. The black star, also from Ghana, is often said to stand for Africa's people and the party's leadership. No law gives the colors a meaning; many read red as blood shed for freedom, yellow as sun and savanna, green as forests and hope.
criticApplied.reason: Date style harmonized to day-month like the rest of the batch; content unchanged. 441 characters.

criticApplied.value: Liberia's flag dates from 24 August 1847 and was sewn by a committee of seven women. It resembles the US flag because Liberia was founded in 1822 as a settlement for free Black Americans. The eleven stripes are said to stand for the eleven signers of the Declaration of Independence, the white star for Africa's first republic, and the blue square for Africa. A 1961 law reads blue as liberty and justice, white as purity, red as courage.
criticApplied.reason: Date style harmonized to day-month like the rest of the batch; content unchanged. 438 characters.

criticApplied.value: Adopted at independence on 11 November 1975, the flag follows that of the MPLA, the party that took power. The constitution says red is the blood shed under colonial rule and in the fight for independence, black is the African continent. The yellow emblem has part of a cogwheel for workers and industry, a machete for farmers and the armed struggle, and a star for international solidarity and progress. Yellow is the country's wealth.
criticApplied.reason: Date style harmonized to day-month like the rest of the batch; content unchanged. 436 characters.

criticApplied.value: Barthélemy Boganda, its first leader, designed the flag, adopted on 1 December 1958. He said its colors stood for the four territories of French Equatorial Africa and for France: blue and white are often linked to France, green and yellow to the Pan-African colors. The red upright stripe is, in his words, the symbol of our blood. Blue is said to mean the sky and freedom, white peace, green hope, yellow tolerance, and the star a bright future.
criticApplied.reason: Date style harmonized to day-month like the rest of the batch; content unchanged. 446 characters.

criticApplied.value: Chad adopted this flag on 6 November 1959, a year before independence from France. The three upright bands copy the shape of the French flag, and yellow and red are Pan-African colors. A first design used green, but blue replaced it so the flag would not match Mali's. The law only names the colors; blue is often said to mean sky and hope, yellow the sun and desert, red unity. Romania's flag is almost identical, but Chad's blue is darker.
criticApplied.reason: Date style harmonized to day-month like the rest of the batch; content unchanged. 441 characters.

criticApplied.value: The flag dates from 15 September 1959, shortly before independence from France. Green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colors shared with Ethiopia, and this is the only Pan-African flag to arrange them diagonally. Green was said to mean farming and forests, yellow the friendship and nobility of the people; red was given no meaning. A Marxist government flew a red flag from 1970 until the original returned on 10 June 1991.
criticApplied.reason: Date style harmonized to day-month like the rest of the batch (two dates); content unchanged. 428 characters.

criticApplied.value: Gabon's flag has three equal bands of green, yellow and blue. The 1959 flag, used while Gabon was still linked to France, had a narrower yellow band and a small French flag in the upper left corner; both changed just before independence in 1960. The constitution gives the colors no meaning. Green is often read as the rainforests covering most of the land, yellow as the sun and the equator that crosses Gabon, and blue as the Atlantic coast.
criticApplied.reason: The text opened with a bare descriptive fragment ('Three equal bands of green, yellow and blue.'); made it a sentence so the paragraph reads as a story rather than a description. 443 characters.

criticApplied.value: Hussein II Bey created the flag around 1831 so Tunisian ships stood out from those of the Ottoman Empire, which then ruled Tunisia. Its red background, crescent and star follow the Ottoman flag. Tunisia's embassy in France says red recalls the blood of its martyrs, the white disc means peace, the crescent Muslim unity and the five star points the five pillars of Islam. The constitution and a 1999 law set its design.
criticApplied.reason: 'The 1959 constitution' is no longer the constitution in force (replaced in 2014 and 2022; the entry's own note records that Article 4 of the 2022 constitution repeats the same description), so the year is dropped to keep the sentence true. 419 characters.
